900.bp: A recommender has to make a useful suggestion for a person who has just arrived and has only a few clicks, watches, purchases, or ratings on record. That is the user cold-start problem: the system cannot safely infer taste from a long history because the history is not there yet. Meta-augmented cold-start recommenders try to solve this by keeping reusable knowledge about common preference patterns, then quickly customizing the model for each new user from a handful of interactions. This paper asks what happens after that first adaptation moment. New users keep arriving in later periods, and their tastes may not match the old common patterns. The recommender therefore has to learn from these later users without losing the reusable patterns that made quick cold-start adaptation possible. IncMCR is aimed at that live setting: recommendation as an ongoing stream of new people and changing preference evidence, not a one-time training problem.
900.wh: The hard part is that the system is pulled in two directions. It must be plastic enough to absorb novel preferences from new users who arrive in later periods, but stable enough to preserve common preference patterns learned earlier for cold-start recommendation. If it changes too little, it treats later users as if they were drawn from the old population and misses fresh taste patterns. If it changes too much, the shared meta-knowledge erodes, meaning the reusable knowledge for fast adaptation is overwritten by recent cases. The abstract also stresses forward compatibility, which is different from merely remembering the past. The model must keep itself in a condition where future new users can still be learned easily. Visual class-incremental learning offers a comparison point, but users are not fixed object classes. Their preferences are sparse, shifting, and expressed through few-shot interaction records, so the system needs continual adaptation without collapsing the cold-start skill it already had.
900.naive: A smart beginner might retrain the cold-start recommender whenever a new period of users arrives. The system would collect those users' few interactions, update the model, and assume the new version is better because it has seen more recent behavior. That fails because recent data is not just extra data; it can pull the model away from older common preference patterns that are still needed for the next cold-start user. Another beginner might freeze the shared knowledge and only customize each user separately. That protects the old base, but it cannot assimilate novel preferences that repeatedly appear in later periods. Both simple choices miss the central tradeoff: the recommender must remember reusable taste structure while also staying ready for preferences it has not yet seen.
900.ap: The core idea is to treat continual cold-start recommendation as managed knowledge evolution. IncMCR does not simply append new user examples to training. It tries to update the shared meta-knowledge in a way that remains forward compatible, meaning the updated knowledge should help future user adaptation rather than only fit the current period. The paper's concrete moves are dual-view forward compatibility adaptation, complementary-oriented meta-task replay, prototype-aware exemplar selection, and a novelty-sensitive meta-updater. In plain terms, it looks at adaptation from two views, replays selected old learning tasks so old shared patterns stay alive, chooses representative examples around prototypes so replay is not random, and makes the updater more sensitive when a retraining period contains genuinely novel preference evidence. The point is not only to prevent forgetting. It is to make each incremental period add new preference structure while preserving the fast-customization machinery for sparse new-user records.
900.mech: The input is a stream of continual periods. In each period, new users arrive with scarce interaction records, and the recommender must adapt from only a few signs of preference. The system begins with meta-knowledge, which means reusable model knowledge learned from prior user-adaptation tasks. First, it forms meta-tasks from user interaction records: each task asks the recommender to adapt quickly for a user or group of similar cold-start situations. During an incremental retraining period, IncMCR updates this shared knowledge using the new period's tasks. Dual-view forward compatibility adaptation checks the update from two complementary angles, so the new knowledge is not judged only by whether it fits the present users but also by whether it remains useful for later adaptation. To avoid meta-knowledge erosion, the method replays older meta-tasks. Replay means bringing selected past tasks back into training, so the model is reminded of common preference patterns that should not be overwritten. Prototype-aware exemplar selection chooses examples that stand for important preference regions rather than arbitrary old records. The complementary-oriented replay then combines these reminders with new tasks. Finally, a novelty-sensitive meta-updater changes how strongly the shared knowledge moves when current users show unfamiliar preferences. The output is an updated cold-start recommender intended to customize quickly for newly arriving users while carrying forward both old common patterns and newly assimilated preference signals.
900.math: The mathematical heart is continual learning, which is learning under time: the rule is updated repeatedly as new batches of evidence arrive, and each update can help or damage future updates. Here the rule is not a single user's taste profile; it is meta-knowledge, reusable knowledge about how to adapt from a few interactions. Optimization, in plain terms, means defining what counts as a bad recommendation or bad adaptation and adjusting model settings to reduce that badness. IncMCR adds a second kind of badness: an update is also bad if it erases common cold-start patterns or leaves the model less prepared for future users. Replay is a sampling idea. Because the system cannot treat all past tasks as equally available or equally useful, it selects exemplars, meaning stored representative cases. Prototype-aware selection uses prototypes, which are central or typical examples of preference regions, so the replay sample covers meaningful old structure. Novelty sensitivity is a weighting idea: evidence that looks unlike existing preference patterns should have enough force to reshape the model, while ordinary evidence should not cause needless drift. The tradeoff is adaptation versus preservation. The math fits because sparse user records make each new case uncertain, while repeated user periods reveal both stable common patterns and real changes that must be folded into the shared rule.
900.dots: This paper sits squarely in the recommender-systems family described in the repo: choosing a small useful set from a huge changing pile when user evidence is partial, delayed, and shaped by the system's own past choices. It connects to cold-start papers because it starts from the same scarcity pressure: new users do not provide enough history for ordinary personalization. It connects to sequence and temporal work because user preference is non-stationary, meaning the order of arriving periods matters and old evidence cannot be treated as equally current forever. It connects to learning-from-examples papers because the system must reuse past cases without copying accidental details. It also connects to optimization because the updater is steering model settings under competing costs: fit new users, preserve common patterns, and remain ready for future users. Neighboring recommendation papers in the batch attack related pressures through cross-scenario incremental samples, cross-domain transfer, promotion-time shifts, and sequence compression. IncMCR's narrower branch is continual cold-start adaptation.
900.ww: The mechanism should improve over naive retraining because it makes forgetting an explicit object of control. Plain retraining sees recent user tasks and moves toward them, even when that movement damages older reusable patterns. IncMCR keeps selected older meta-tasks in the update loop, so the model has to satisfy reminders of what made quick cold-start adaptation work before. Prototype-aware exemplar selection matters because replay is only useful if the stored cases cover important preference structure. If replay used arbitrary examples, it could overprotect rare accidents or miss central patterns. The novelty-sensitive updater addresses the opposite danger. A preservation-heavy model can become too conservative, treating genuinely new preference patterns as noise. By increasing sensitivity when a period contains novel preferences, the model can absorb new structure rather than only defend old structure. Forward compatibility ties these pieces together: the update is judged by whether it leaves the model useful for later new-user adaptation. The expected gain comes from balancing three signals at once: current scarce interactions, representative old tasks, and evidence that the preference world has shifted.
900.po: The payoff is a cold-start recommender that is meant for dynamic streaming environments rather than a static training snapshot. It can assimilate novel preferences from new users arriving over continual periods while preserving common preference patterns extracted for cold-start recommendation. In practical terms, this buys a recommendation system that can keep learning as user populations change without repeatedly sacrificing the fast few-shot customization skill that helped newcomers in the first place. The abstract claims IncMCR improves meta-knowledge evolution with dual-view forward compatibility adaptation, combats meta-knowledge erosion through selected replay, and strengthens novelty assimilation through a novelty-sensitive updater.
900.limits: Several assumptions have to hold. The few-shot interaction records must contain enough signal to reveal preference rather than accidental exposure, promotion effects, or noise from the recommender's previous choices. The selected prototypes must truly represent useful old preference regions; if they are biased or stale, replay can preserve the wrong habits. Novelty detection must distinguish real new preference patterns from temporary spikes. The abstract names IncMCR's components but does not provide datasets, metrics, comparison details, or long-term deployment evidence in the provided text. It also does not prove effects on fairness, privacy, user welfare, or cases where future users differ sharply from every stored prototype.

901.bp: A language-model agent becomes useful only when it can turn a user's request into the right outside action. The outside action might be calling a calculator, searching a database, opening an API, or using a specialized tool that the model itself does not contain. This paper studies the gate between language and action: given a request and a changing set of available tools, the agent must pick the tool that can actually move the task forward. The need appears before any training method is named because tool use is no longer a small demonstration problem. Real tool logs are uneven, messy, and incomplete. Common tools appear often, specialized tools appear rarely, some examples are only partly correct, and the tool inventory can change. TOOL-CURE is aimed at making a tool-selection agent learn from that imperfect world instead of requiring a clean, balanced classroom of perfect query-tool pairs.
901.wh: The hard part is that tool selection asks the model to learn a moving map between user intent and tool capability. A user query may not use the same words as the tool description, and a tool may be rare enough that the training data contains only a few examples. The abstract says the data follow a long-tail pattern: a few tools dominate while many specialized tools are scarce. It also says some examples contain logic conflicts between the user query and available tools, and some samples are partially correct or dirty. That means the training signal is not just small; it can be misleading. Standard supervised fine-tuning treats every labeled example as if it were ground truth, so bad labels teach bad habits. Plain reward-based learning tries to learn from outcomes, but the paper says vanilla GRPO can become unstable when rewards conflict or when weak signals do not clearly teach which tool choice was responsible.
901.naive: A smart beginner would collect examples of user queries paired with the tool that was used, then train the model to imitate those pairings. This is supervised fine-tuning: show the model many labeled cases and ask it to repeat the label for similar future cases. That fails when the example pile is not trustworthy. If most examples involve popular tools, the model learns to over-choose them and under-learns rare specialized tools. If some labels are only partly right, the model copies the mistake. If tools change, memorized query-tool pairs age quickly. A second naive move is to use rewards directly, but the abstract says plain GRPO suffers from unstable updates when reward signals disagree or are too weak.
901.ap: TOOL-CURE keeps the reward-based idea but changes the training environment so the model is not thrown into the mess all at once. Its first move, Proficiency-Scaled Curriculum Learning, arranges learning into stages. The agent first practices on easier samples where the correct tool choice is more learnable, then moves to harder samples after it has built basic skill. The point is not just convenience; it reduces the chance that rare, conflicting, or noisy cases dominate before the model has a stable sense of what tool choice means. Its second move, Online Policy Guarding via Sample Screening, watches the quality of training rollouts while learning is happening. When samples look dirty or likely to send the update in a harmful direction, the method masks them so they do not drive the policy change. The central move is staged practice plus active filtering of bad teaching signals.
901.mech: The input is a real-world tool-selection training set: user queries, available tools, labels or outcomes tied to tool choices, and examples with uneven quality. The method starts from GRPO, a reward-based training rule where the model tries several actions, receives scores for how well those actions worked, compares alternatives within a group, and changes its behavior toward choices that scored better. TOOL-CURE modifies that process in two places. First, the curriculum component separates training into an easier phase and a harder phase. In the easier phase, the model learns foundational matching behavior: notice what the user is asking for, connect that need to tool capability, and avoid obvious mismatches. After that, it is exposed to more difficult cases where tools are rare, examples are less direct, or the query-tool relation is harder to infer. Second, the sample-screening component evaluates rollout quality during training. A rollout is one attempted path from query to tool choice and resulting reward. If the sample appears dirty, partially correct, or likely to produce a noisy update, the method masks it from the update. What comes out is a trained tool-selection policy: a model behavior that should choose tools more accurately and generalize better than plain imitation or unguarded GRPO.
901.math: The main mathematics is decision learning from feedback. The model has many possible actions, namely tool choices, and it must change the chance of choosing each action based on evidence from outcomes. Reinforcement learning is the idea of learning a behavior by rewarding actions that lead to better results, rather than copying a fixed label. GRPO is a particular way to compare several attempted choices and update the policy, where a policy means the model's current tendency to pick one action over another. The risk is that an update is only as good as the signal that caused it. If a bad sample says the wrong tool is good, the math confidently walks in the wrong direction. Curriculum learning adds an ordering principle: learn easier cases before harder ones so the early updates form a stable base. Sample screening adds a filtering principle: not every observed reward should be trusted equally. Masking dirty samples is a way of saying that some evidence is too corrupted to use. The tradeoff is learning from messy real data versus protecting the learner from noise that would bend the decision rule toward wrong tools.
901.dots: This paper sits in the LLM agent tool-use theme because it studies the moment where a language model stops only writing text and chooses an outside capability. It connects to retrieval and ranking because tool selection is a small ranking problem: from many possible tools, put the useful one on top. It connects to similarity because the system must compare a user's need with tool capabilities even when their wording differs. It also belongs to the reinforcement-learning family in the repo's current data, alongside papers that use downstream usefulness as the teaching signal for search, tool use, summarization, or agent behavior. TOOL-CURE's distinctive pressure is the quality of the teaching signal itself. Neighboring agent papers often ask how to retrieve a tool, call a search system, or route a task cheaply. This paper asks how to train the chooser when the historical examples are imbalanced, scarce, conflicting, and dirty.
901.ww: The method should help because the two additions attack two different failure sources. The curriculum addresses difficulty ordering. If the model begins with the hardest and noisiest cases, early updates may be pulled by accidental patterns: choose the popular tool, copy a flawed label, or overreact to a weak reward. Easier cases give the model repeated, clearer evidence about the basic relation between a request and a tool. Once that relation is partly learned, harder examples become less chaotic because the model has a reference point for what a plausible choice looks like. The screening step addresses evidence quality. Reward-based learning can be powerful because it learns from success, but it can also mistake dirty feedback for real success. By assessing rollout quality and masking bad samples, TOOL-CURE reduces the amount of corrupted evidence entering the update. Together, staged practice and guarded updates make the learning process less likely to amplify rare-label scarcity, partial correctness, or logical conflicts in the data.
901.po: The payoff is a tool-selection agent that can learn from heterogeneous real-world data instead of depending on abundant clean labels. According to the abstract, TOOL-CURE improves GRPO with proficiency-scaled curriculum learning and online sample screening, producing more stable and efficient learning. The practical capability is better selection of external tools for language-model agents, especially when the tool set is imbalanced, specialized tools are scarce, and some training cases are dirty. The abstract reports significant improvements in accuracy and generalization capability, so the claimed gain is not merely fitting old query-tool pairs but choosing tools better in cases beyond the exact training examples.
901.limits: The abstract does not show the datasets, metrics, or error cases, so the strength of the claim depends on details outside this input. The method assumes that easier and harder samples can be organized in a useful curriculum, and that rollout quality can be assessed well enough to identify dirty samples without discarding valuable rare cases. It also assumes the reward signal is aligned with genuinely useful tool choice. If the reward favors superficial success, the model may still learn shortcuts. Rapidly evolving toolsets remain a challenge because new tools may lack examples. The abstract reports accuracy and generalization gains, but it does not prove safety under adversarial tool descriptions, poisoned logs, or changing user goals.

902.bp: This paper is about noticing real events as they surface through social media posts, where each post may contain both an image and a short piece of text. The ordinary need is practical: public safety and social governance depend on seeing that many scattered posts are actually pointing to the same thing happening in the world. A crowd gathering, a road accident, or a local emergency may not arrive as a neat database record. It arrives as photos, captions, fragments, slang, and reposts. The paper focuses on the open-world version of this problem, where the system is not handed a fixed list of event names and is not given supervised event labels. Its proposed system, LFEvent, tries to discover event groupings directly from raw image-text pairs by enriching their meaning and then learning which pairs should sit close together across visual and textual evidence.
902.wh: The hard part is that social media is both messy and open-ended. A supervised detector needs examples already marked with event labels, but the paper says open-world social media often lacks those labels and also lacks structured information. Even worse, many detectors assume the total number of event categories is known before detection begins. That assumption fits a classroom exercise better than a live social stream. In the real world, new events appear, old labels may not cover them, and the same event can be described in many ways. Images and text also do not match perfectly: a caption may be vague while the image carries the useful clue, or the image may be ambiguous until the text gives context. The central tension is therefore between needing stable groupings and having no reliable event names, no known event count, and two different media types that must be compared fairly.
902.naive: A smart beginner might collect posts, write a list of event types such as accident, protest, concert, and disaster, label examples for each type, and train a classifier to assign each new post to one of those boxes. If labels are unavailable, the beginner might instead group posts by surface similarity: captions with shared words go together, and images that look visually similar go together. Both attempts break in the setting described by the paper. The labeled classifier cannot detect an event type that was never included in the list, and it depends on costly labels. The surface grouping can confuse posts that use similar words for different events or miss posts where the image and text reveal the event only when read together.
902.ap: The paper's central move is to create useful training signals without human event labels. LFEvent starts from raw image-text pairs and asks a multimodal large language model to enrich each pair along three event-centered dimensions: the event theme, the event type, and the image description. In plain terms, it turns a sparse post into a fuller description of what the post seems to be about, what kind of event it may show, and what is visible in the picture. These enriched versions become positive samples, meaning different views that should agree about the same underlying post or event cue. A Siamese Network, which is a pair of matching processing paths that learn to judge closeness, then learns cross-modal alignment: images and text are arranged so matching event meaning is near, even without manually supplied labels.
902.mech: The mechanism begins with one raw social media item containing an image and text. First, LFEvent uses carefully crafted prompts with a multimodal large language model, a model that can reason over both pictures and words, to produce semantic enhancements. The local input says these enhancements cover event theme, event type, and image description. That step changes a thin post into several richer descriptions centered on event meaning rather than only surface pixels or words. Next, these enriched image-text materials are treated as positive samples. A positive sample is not a human label; it is an internally generated partner that should preserve the same event signal. Then the Siamese Network processes paired views through matched branches so the system can learn a shared comparison rule. During self-supervised cross-modal alignment, the model is pushed to place image-derived and text-derived evidence for the same post or event meaning close together. It is also learning a representation, meaning a compact numeric description, but the important ordinary idea is simpler: each post is turned into a location on a map where nearness should mean event-related likeness. Once that map exists, event detection can be treated as finding groups of nearby posts. The output is not a label chosen from a predefined set; it is a discovered event structure suitable for an open world where the number of events is difficult to estimate.
902.math: The main mathematical idea is learning by comparison. Instead of telling the system the correct event name, the method creates paired views that should agree and trains the model to make their descriptions close. This is contrastive learning, which means building a comparison map by pulling together things that are supposed to match and, in general, keeping nonmatching things from collapsing into the same place. The paper emphasizes relying solely on positive samples, so the strongest grounded claim is that LFEvent learns from agreement among enriched views rather than from labeled classes. A second idea is similarity as distance in a learned space. A post, its image description, its event theme, and its textual cues are compressed into numbers; nearby numbers are treated as evidence of related event meaning. A third idea is cross-modal alignment. Images and text begin as different kinds of objects, like photographs and sentences, so their raw forms cannot be directly compared. Alignment builds a shared measuring surface where a visual cue and a phrase can support the same event. The Siamese design supplies symmetry: two matched branches learn a common rule for comparing paired inputs. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. The map must keep event-relevant information while discarding wording, background objects, or visual clutter that should not define the event.
902.dots: This paper sits at the crossing of multimodal vision-language work, self-supervised learning, similarity, and social media mining. It shares the multimodal problem with systems that must combine pictures and words rather than trust either source alone. It shares the self-supervised pressure with papers that lack clean labels and therefore manufacture learning signals from the structure already inside the data. It also belongs to the similarity family: the practical act after learning is to decide which posts are close enough in event meaning to belong together. The local family data names neighboring work such as multimodal recommendation and sensor-to-text alignment, which use the same broader move of making different evidence types comparable. LFEvent applies that move to open-world event detection. Its special pressure is the unknown event count: retrieval or recommendation can often rank known candidates, but this task must discover groupings when the future list of events has not been written yet.
902.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it attacks the two stated failures directly. When labels are missing, it does not wait for people to annotate event categories; it asks a multimodal language model to produce event-centered descriptions from the raw image-text pair. That gives the learner richer anchors than raw captions or pixels alone. When the number of events is unknown, it avoids forcing every post into a fixed label set. By learning a map of event likeness, it leaves room for new clusters to appear. The semantic enhancement is useful because real events usually have several connected traces: a theme, a possible event type, visible objects or actions, and words people use around the scene. If these traces are made explicit, unrelated variation becomes less dominant. The Siamese cross-modal alignment then makes image evidence and text evidence answer the same comparison question. A post with vague text but a clear image, or the reverse, can still be positioned by shared event meaning rather than by only one weak channel.
902.po: The payoff is an unsupervised route to multimodal social event detection in a live, open setting. Grounded in the local abstract and analysis data, LFEvent buys three capabilities: it reduces dependence on supervised event labels, it does not require a predefined total number of event categories, and it uses both image and text evidence through semantic enrichment and cross-modal alignment. That matters because social media events are dynamic. A useful detector should adapt when new events appear and when posts provide incomplete clues. The paper's claimed contribution is therefore not merely a better classifier, but a way to discover event structure from unlabeled multimodal posts.
902.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The multimodal language model must produce useful event theme, event type, and image-description enrichments; if those descriptions are wrong or overly generic, the positive samples may teach the wrong likeness. The raw image-text pairs must contain enough shared event signal for alignment to find groups. The learned map must preserve event meaning rather than popularity, repeated wording, visual background, or posting style. The local abstract is truncated, so it does not show evaluation details, datasets, or the exact method for handling unknown event counts. It also does not prove performance under adversarial posts, rumors, duplicated content, rare events, or events whose images and captions intentionally mislead.

903.bp: A short-video advertising platform has to decide, for each user and advertiser, how likely an ad click is to turn into a real purchase or other conversion. On ordinary days, yesterday's behavior is often a useful teacher: people browse, click, and buy in roughly familiar rhythms. Large shopping promotions break that rhythm. Around Black Friday or 618 Shopping Day, users wait for discounts, advertisers change bids and campaigns, traffic composition changes, and the meaning of a click can shift sharply. TemporalExpertNet serves this practical moment. It is trying to keep conversion-rate prediction useful when the platform enters a known but unusual season. The paper treats promotion periods not as random noise, but as recurring temporal regimes with reusable knowledge. Its goal is to reuse what was learned from earlier promotion cycles while still adapting to the current users, advertisers, and features on a large short-video ads platform.
903.wh: The hard part is that promotion behavior changes in uneven ways. Some patterns stay stable: a user's broad interests, an advertiser's product category, and general ad-response clues may still matter. Other patterns become promotion-sensitive: users may delay buying until the sale, advertisers may push different creatives, and the same feature value can mean something different during preheating than during a normal day. A single daily model tends to mix these two kinds of evidence into one set of learned habits. If it trusts normal-day patterns too much, it underreacts to the sale. If it overfits one old promotion, it may reuse stale behavior when the current promotion has different shoppers or advertisers. The abstract also says the shifts are heterogeneous, which means not every sample needs the same adjustment. The model therefore needs both temporal reuse and sample-level caution: borrow the right historical knowledge, align it with current features, and decide case by case how much of it to use.
903.naive: A smart beginner might train a strong conversion model on daily data, then keep using it through the promotion. That fails because the training examples mostly describe ordinary behavior, while the sale period changes both user intent and advertiser strategy. Another beginner fix is to train a separate model for each promotion period. That can capture sale-specific behavior, but it wastes repeated structure across promotions and may be weak when the current promotion has limited fresh labels. A third fix is to fine-tune the old model on current data. The abstract suggests this is still too rigid because historical knowledge and current features may not line up cleanly, and different samples need different mixes of stable and promotion-sensitive knowledge.
903.ap: TemporalExpertNet's central move is to split the predictor into parts with different jobs. One part is a stable representation encoder: it tries to preserve the recurring signals that remain useful across time, such as broad user, ad, and context patterns. Another part is a promotion-sensitive expert: it focuses on the behavior that changes during promotion cycles. The paper then adds two bridges between past and present. BridgeNet handles the mismatch between historical temporal knowledge and current features by aligning their internal descriptions, so old promotion knowledge is not pasted onto the present in the wrong coordinate system. TemporalExpertGate performs sample-aware expert fusion, meaning it chooses, for each example, how much to trust different expert knowledge. The method is therefore not simply a bigger predictor. It is a controlled reuse machine: keep stable signals, adapt sale-sensitive signals, and gate their mixture according to the current sample.
903.mech: The mechanism starts with logged advertising examples from ordinary days and promotion periods. Each example contains current features about a user, advertiser, ad situation, and later conversion outcome. First, the stable encoder turns the raw features into a compact description meant to carry patterns that should survive across time. This is the part the system wants to reuse rather than relearn from scratch for every sale. Next, the promotion-sensitive expert models the part of the prediction that changes when a promotion cycle alters browsing and buying behavior. Historical promotion knowledge cannot simply be copied, because feature meanings and population mix can change. BridgeNet therefore aligns the historical temporal description with the current feature description, reducing the mismatch between what the old promotion expert knows and what the present sample looks like. Then TemporalExpertGate reads the sample and decides how to fuse expert outputs. For one user-ad pair, the stable encoder may be enough; for another, a sale-specific expert may deserve more weight. Training happens in two stages, according to the abstract: first to make alignment stable, then to learn adaptive expert fusion. The output is a conversion-rate score used by the ads platform to rank or allocate impressions during the 618 preheating phase.
903.math: The mathematical ideas are learning from examples, temporal transfer, alignment, weighted expert mixing, and error reduction. Learning from examples means the system sees many past cases where features were followed by conversion or no conversion, then learns a scoring rule that gives higher scores to cases that looked like later converters. Temporal transfer means reusing patterns from an earlier time period because the current period has a related shape. The danger is false reuse: yesterday's sale knowledge may be close enough to help, or different enough to hurt. Alignment is the mathematical repair for that danger. It changes internal descriptions from historical and current data so comparable cases are brought into a shared language before they are reused. Expert mixing means several specialized predictors produce advice, and a gate assigns weights to their advice for each sample. A weight is a controlled amount of trust, not a permanent rule. The two-stage training is an error-reduction process: define what counts as a bad alignment or bad conversion prediction, then adjust model settings to reduce that badness. The tradeoff is stability versus adaptability. Keep too much stable knowledge and the sale shift is missed; trust the promotion expert too much and current predictions may chase short-lived noise.
903.dots: This paper sits where recommendation, advertising, ranking, and time-aware prediction meet. Like other conversion-rate papers in the repo, such as ChorusCVR and discount-aware CVR modeling, it asks why a click or ad impression should be trusted as evidence of later buying. Its special pressure is time: the same marketplace behaves differently during promotion cycles. That connects it to the time-series family, where the recurring lesson is that past structure helps only after the system separates stable rhythm from sudden change. It also connects to mixture-of-experts ideas in commerce, such as delayed GMV prediction with routing, because both split cases that should not be averaged into one predictor. At the platform level, the predicted conversion rate becomes part of ranking and ad allocation: which ad deserves scarce exposure now? TemporalExpertNet's answer is that ranking during a sale should not be driven by a flat daily model, but by a temporally adjusted score that knows when old promotion knowledge is relevant.
903.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach because it matches the actual shape of promotion data. Promotions are not completely new worlds, so throwing away old knowledge is wasteful. They are also not ordinary days, so treating all history as equally current is misleading. By separating a stable encoder from a promotion-sensitive expert, the model gives each kind of evidence a proper place. BridgeNet helps because reuse only works when the thing being reused is compared in the same internal language as the current sample. If historical promotion patterns and present features are misaligned, the model may apply a past rule to the wrong kind of user or advertiser. The gate helps because heterogeneous shifts mean no single adjustment is right for everyone. A bargain hunter in a sale category may need strong promotion-specific correction, while another user-ad pair may still follow ordinary behavior. Sample-aware fusion lets the model vary that trust continuously. The reported small model-size and latency overhead also matter: the mechanism is useful only if it can run inside an industrial ads system without slowing serving too much.
903.po: The payoff is a promotion-aware conversion predictor that can be deployed rather than only studied offline. The abstract reports that TemporalExpertNet was used on a large short-video ads platform during the 618 preheating phase. It improved conversion rate by 7.52 percent and platform revenue per mille by 4.27 percent, while adding only 0.23 percent model size and 1.8 percent latency overhead. In practical terms, the system buys better sale-period ad ranking with modest serving cost. It lets the platform reuse past promotion knowledge without assuming every promotion, user, and advertiser behaves identically.
903.limits: Several assumptions must hold. Past promotion cycles must contain knowledge that is genuinely reusable for the current cycle; if the current sale has different products, policies, users, discounts, or advertiser tactics, transfer can mislead. BridgeNet assumes historical and current descriptions can be aligned well enough for reuse. The gate assumes the model has enough evidence to decide which expert to trust for each sample. The abstract reports deployment during one 618 preheating phase on a short-video ads platform, but it does not prove the same gains for other platforms, sale types, countries, or longer post-sale periods. It also reports business metrics, not detailed failure analysis for minority advertisers, cold-start campaigns, or adversarial promotion behavior.

904.bp: A large shopping homepage cannot examine every product for every visitor in real time. It first uses several fast retrieval models, each acting like a different scout that brings back a small pile of possible items before a later ranker sorts them more carefully. This parallel design is useful because one scout may cover recent behavior, another may cover cross-scenario signals from a different part of the platform, and another may cover broad popular interest. The paper starts from a practical waste inside that design: when an added cross-scenario retriever mostly brings back products that older retrievers already found, the system has spent extra computation but has not expanded the useful candidate pool much. IncRec is meant for Taobao-style homepage recommendation, where the valuable question is not only whether an item is relevant, but whether it adds something the current retrieval system would otherwise miss.
904.wh: The hard part is that relevance and incrementality are not the same goal. A product can be highly relevant to a user and still be unhelpful as training evidence for a new retriever if the existing system already retrieves it. Adding more cross-scenario samples then gives a tempting but shallow improvement path: the new model learns from many good examples, yet many of those examples teach it to repeat work already done by other models. At large scale, this creates diminishing marginal utility. Each extra retrieval path may look strong on its own while adding little to the combined system. The paper also has to avoid the opposite mistake. If the new retriever only chases items that no existing model finds, it may drift toward obscure products that technically fill a gap but are unlikely to be shown or acted on. The tension is between finding missed candidates and keeping candidates that have real exposure probability.
904.naive: A smart beginner would add cross-scenario data to the retrieval model and train it to find items users clicked, bought, or otherwise responded to in those other scenarios. If some extra data is good, more extra data seems better. The failure is overlap. Many of those cross-scenario examples may already be reachable by retrievers in the deployed system, so the new model learns to recover candidates the system already has. Another beginner fix would be to filter duplicate retrieved items after retrieval. That removes visible repetition, but it does not teach the new model what kind of unseen candidate is worth finding. It treats redundancy as a cleanup problem instead of a learning problem.
904.ap: IncRec changes the target of learning from generally good cross-scenario samples to incremental cross-scenario samples. In plain terms, it asks: among examples from other scenarios, which ones are valuable precisely because none of the current retrieval models would have found them? The paper calls these extreme cross-scenario incremental samples. The model then learns a representation, meaning a compact numeric description of user and item signals, that is specialized for this missing portion of the candidate space rather than for the already covered portion. A second piece, the consistency-aware alignment module, keeps the search from becoming novelty for its own sake. It makes the model prefer incremental samples that are also consistent with high exposure probability, so the candidate is not merely different from current retrievals but plausibly useful in the homepage recommendation flow.
904.mech: The input is a deployed multi-retrieval recommendation setting: existing retrieval models, cross-scenario samples, and user-item evidence from the platform. First, the system uses the existing retrievers as a boundary marker. A cross-scenario sample that is already retrieved by any existing model is treated as less useful for the specific goal of adding new coverage. A sample missed by all existing models becomes an extreme incremental sample, because it marks a part of user interest not currently brought forward. Second, IncRec trains a retrieval model around these missed samples. It must turn user context and item information into compact descriptions that can be compared quickly, so items matching the uncovered interest pattern rise into the candidate set. Third, the consistency-aware alignment module checks the incremental direction against exposure probability. Exposure probability is the chance that an item is likely enough to surface or matter in the real recommendation environment. The output is not the final homepage order. It is a better retrieval candidate pool: fewer redundant candidates, more missed-but-plausible candidates, and therefore a richer set for downstream ranking. The abstract reports offline tests, online A/B tests, and deployment on Taobao's homepage.
904.math: The main mathematical idea is ranking under a coverage constraint. Ranking means giving candidate items scores so a huge pile can be sorted into a small usable set. Here the score cannot mean ordinary relevance alone, because ordinary relevance may duplicate what existing retrievers already recover. The model needs a second notion: incremental value, which is the value of an item conditional on the current system not already finding it. This is like asking how much new information a candidate adds after accounting for what is already known. The representation part is a learned compression: user and item evidence are squeezed into numeric descriptions so closeness or compatibility can be computed quickly. The danger of compression is that it can preserve the wrong similarity, such as general popularity instead of missed user interest. The alignment module adds a probability idea. Probability here means estimating uncertainty about exposure: among the missed samples, which ones have signs that they can realistically appear and contribute? The tradeoff is novelty versus usefulness, and the optimization loop is the process of adjusting model settings so retrieved candidates are both uncovered by old models and likely to be valuable.
904.dots: This paper sits inside the conference's recurring problem of choosing a small useful set from a huge candidate universe. It is connected to ranking because the final practical act is still score, sort, and pass forward only a few items. It is connected to similarity because retrieval depends on placing users and items near each other when their evidence suggests a match. It is connected to optimization because the system must decide what counts as a better retriever: not the one that looks best alone, but the one that improves the combined retrieval architecture. Within recommender systems, it is a sibling of work on multi-objective recommendation, cold-start transfer, and long-tail visibility, because all of them fight the same hidden failure: a model can be accurate by repeating easy, visible, already-served patterns. IncRec's narrower contribution is to make the gap left by existing retrievers the object being learned.
904.ww: IncRec should work when the existing retrieval system has real overlap. In that case, training on all good cross-scenario samples wastes part of the learning signal on already solved cases. By constructing samples that no current model retrieves, the method points the new model at the uncovered remainder. That changes the role of the new retriever from another general-purpose scout into a specialist for missing candidates. The consistency-aware alignment piece matters because missing candidates are not automatically good candidates. Some are missed because they are unusual, weakly connected to user demand, or unlikely to be exposed. Aligning the incremental samples with high exposure probability filters the missing set toward items that can plausibly affect the live system. The intuitive reason is marginal value: the first model to find an item creates value, while the fifth model finding the same item adds little. A model trained to add distinct, plausible candidates increases the quality of the combined pool even if its isolated retrieval list is not the whole story.
904.po: The payoff is a retrieval system that treats additional cross-scenario data as a way to expand coverage, not just as more examples to memorize. The abstract reports that IncRec is validated through offline tests and online A/B tests, then deployed in Taobao homepage recommendation. The repo's current analysis records the headline outcome as a 1% increase in online transaction count. In product terms, that means the method buys more useful candidate discovery before final ranking, using the same basic multi-retrieval architecture but reducing wasted overlap among retrieval paths.
904.limits: The claim depends on the current retrieval system having measurable redundancy. If existing models already cover mostly distinct candidate regions, the incremental target may be smaller. It also depends on correctly identifying which samples are not retrieved by any existing model; if that logging or matching is incomplete, the training target becomes noisy. Exposure probability must be a trustworthy proxy for practical usefulness, not merely another form of historical popularity. The abstract does not prove how IncRec behaves for smaller platforms, different item catalogs, new scenarios with little cross-scenario data, or settings where novelty conflicts with fairness, diversity, or user satisfaction beyond transaction count.

905.bp: A recommender often has too little evidence in the place where it must make a choice. A bookstore may know many reading habits, while a music or movie service may have only a few ratings for the same kind of user or item. Cross-domain recommendation tries to borrow knowledge from a richer domain to help a poorer one. DDIREC serves that practical need, but it begins from a warning: shared words in item descriptions are not automatically shared meaning. A word can look general across domains while pointing to different buying reasons inside each domain. If the system transfers that word blindly, it may recommend the wrong items with great confidence. This paper is about making item descriptions travel more carefully. It separates words into domain-specific, domain-shared, and domain-independent roles, then uses an item-topic-word graph to build item representations that transfer useful meaning while reducing harmful transfer.
905.wh: The hard part is that cross-domain data is both helpful and dangerous. Sparse domains need outside evidence, but outside evidence comes from a different world of items, words, user habits, and meanings. A word in an item description may appear in both domains, yet its practical meaning can shift. For example, the abstract does not give domains, but the same descriptive term could signal style in one catalog and function in another. Existing methods struggle with domain-independent information that appears shared but carries domain-specific meanings. That creates negative transfer, where borrowed evidence hurts the target domain instead of helping it. The system therefore must answer a more delicate question than whether two domains share vocabulary. It must ask how each word behaves inside topics, whether items using that word lean toward one domain, and whether passing that signal to another domain preserves meaning or smuggles in a local habit.
905.naive: A smart beginner would collect item descriptions from all domains, find common words or topics, and treat them as bridges. If many items mention the same word, the recommender could assume that those items share a preference signal and train one common item description from them. This fails because shared surface language can hide different uses. A word that seems domain-independent may still be skewed toward items from one domain inside a topic, meaning it is not neutral evidence. The beginner method also treats all shared words alike, so it cannot separate a word that truly carries transferable meaning from one that only looks transferable because the vocabularies overlap. The result is false sameness, and false sameness leads to negative transfer.
905.ap: DDIREC's central move is to split the language of item descriptions before transfer happens. Instead of asking only whether a word appears across domains, it asks how words are distributed inside topics and how strongly the items connected to those words lean toward a particular domain. That skewness, meaning imbalance toward one domain rather than an even spread, lets the method sort words into three roles. Domain-specific words should mostly stay local. Domain-shared words can carry useful common meaning. Domain-independent words need special care because they may look broadly applicable while still carrying domain-flavored meaning in a topic. After this sorting, DDIREC builds a graph whose places are items, topics, and words, with different kinds of links among them. A graph neural network, meaning a learned rule that lets connected places exchange evidence, then creates item representations for rating prediction and ranking.
905.mech: The input is item-description text from more than one recommendation domain, along with the recommendation task in which items must be rated or ranked. DDIREC first looks at descriptions through topics, where a topic is a repeated bundle of words that tends to describe a common aspect of items. Within each topic, it checks the skewness of items toward a domain. In plain terms, it asks whether the items connected to a word or topic are mostly coming from one domain or are more evenly spread. That check is used to categorize words as domain-specific, domain-shared, or domain-independent. The method then constructs an item-topic-word graph. Items connect to the topics and words that describe them; topics connect to the words that help define them; and the graph keeps these as different kinds of places and relationships rather than flattening everything into one bag of words. A heterogeneous graph neural network, meaning a network-learning model built for several types of places and links, repeatedly updates each item's description from its connected topics and words. Because the word roles have been separated, the evidence passed through the graph is meant to emphasize transferable meaning and dampen misleading local meaning. The output is an item representation, a compact learned description of the item, used by the recommender to predict ratings and produce ranked lists.
905.math: The first mathematical idea is categorization by imbalance. Skewness here means measuring whether the items attached to a topic or word lean strongly toward one domain. A perfectly even spread would suggest broader use; a strong lean suggests local meaning. This is probability-like reasoning from counts: repeated observations of where words appear change how much the system trusts them as transferable evidence. The second idea is graph reasoning. The graph has different kinds of nodes, meaning places on the map: items, topics, and words. Its links say that an item uses a word, a topic contains a word, or an item belongs near a topic. A heterogeneous graph neural network is a learned message-passing rule for such a mixed map. Each node keeps a compact list of numbers, an item representation, that records what the model currently knows. Connected nodes send information to one another, and the rule learns how much to accept from each type of neighbor. The third idea is ranking and rating prediction. The final item descriptions are scored so the system can estimate a rating or order candidates. The central tradeoff is transfer versus contamination. Share too little and the sparse domain stays sparse; share too much and domain-specific meanings leak across boundaries.
905.dots: This paper sits in the recommender-systems family because it is trying to choose useful items from a large catalog when direct evidence is thin. It connects to the repo's similarity idea: the recommender needs item descriptions where closeness means transferable user meaning, not merely shared vocabulary. It connects to graph learning because DDIREC explicitly builds an item-topic-word graph and lets evidence move through typed links. It also connects to ranking because the final test is not just whether item descriptions look clean, but whether they help rating prediction and ranked recommendation. Nearby cross-domain papers in the repo face the same deeper pressure from different angles. FeDecider separates shared update direction from domain-specific scale in federated recommendation. S2CDR uses item-item relations to transfer cold-start preference. SimTranGCN uses cross-domain similarity matrices. DDIREC's branch is semantic: it asks which words in item text should be allowed to carry meaning across domains.
905.ww: DDIREC should work over the naive approach because it attacks the main source of harm before the recommender starts scoring items. The naive approach treats overlap as trust: if a word or topic appears in several places, it becomes a bridge. DDIREC asks whether that bridge is actually carrying the same meaning. By checking domain skewness inside topics, it can notice when an apparently broad word is mostly tied to one domain's items. That gives the graph-learning step cleaner evidence to pass around. The graph also helps because item meaning is not stored in one word. An item is described by a pattern of words and topics, and those pieces can support or correct one another. When the graph neural network updates item representations through typed links, it can combine local description, topic context, and word-role information instead of forcing all text into one undifferentiated vector of numbers. The intuitive gain is controlled borrowing: the sparse domain still receives outside help, but the help has been filtered by how words behave across domains.
905.po: The payoff is a more careful cross-domain recommender for sparse and cold-start settings. DDIREC lets domains borrow item-description knowledge without assuming that every shared or general-looking word should transfer. The abstract reports that, by categorizing words and learning through an item-topic-word graph, the method properly transfers knowledge while reducing negative transfer. It also says experiments show consistent gains over baselines in both rating prediction and ranking. Practically, that means better estimates of how much a user may like an item and better ordered recommendation lists when one domain lacks enough direct interaction data.
905.limits: The method assumes item descriptions contain enough meaningful words to reveal transferable and nontransferable item structure. It also assumes the topic construction and skewness measurement are reliable: if topics are noisy, too broad, or built from biased descriptions, the word categories may be wrong. The abstract does not say which domains, datasets, or user groups were tested, so the breadth of the evidence cannot be judged from this input alone. The graph approach also depends on links between items, topics, and words being informative rather than accidental. DDIREC reduces negative transfer as reported, but the abstract does not prove that all domain-independent words can be safely identified or that the categories remain stable when item language changes over time.

906.bp: Start with a large social network: each person, account, page, or device is a node, and each relationship is a link. A platform, analyst, or scientist may want to know which nodes matter most because those nodes are good places to watch information spread, recommend contacts, detect influence, or understand the shape of the community. Katz centrality is one way to answer that question. Instead of counting only direct neighbors, it gives credit for many paths through the graph, with shorter and more numerous paths usually making a node look more important. That is useful because influence is rarely only one hop away. A person can matter because many paths eventually lead to them or from them. The paper serves the practical problem that this richer importance score becomes too expensive on large graphs. The goal is to keep the useful ranking signal of Katz centrality while making the computation fast enough for real graph sizes.
906.wh: The hard part is that Katz centrality asks a global question. A node's score is not determined only by its immediate links. It depends on walks through the network, so changing or counting evidence in one region can affect scores elsewhere. Computing the exact answer can require work comparable to multiplying large graph matrices, and the abstract says this can reach cubic time. In plain terms, if the graph grows, the direct calculation can grow so quickly that it stops being usable. Existing approximations already recognize that exactness is too costly, but the abstract says most of them do not exploit parallelism well. That matters because modern machines often have many cores or many workers. If an approximation forces workers to wait on each other, it wastes available hardware. The central tension is therefore accuracy versus cost: the method must preserve enough centrality information to rank influential nodes, while avoiding a calculation whose price rises too sharply with graph size.
906.naive: A smart beginner would first compute Katz centrality exactly. They would build the graph, count the weighted contribution of paths, and give every node its final importance score. That is conceptually clean because it follows the definition directly. It fails because direct faithfulness is too expensive when the graph is large; the abstract says exact computation can be prohibitively costly, up to cubic time. A second beginner move would be to use any available approximate method and hope the answer is close enough. That also fails when the approximation is not built for parallel work. Large graphs need many independent pieces of work running at the same time. If the approximation has bottlenecks, it may still be too slow even though it is less exact.
906.ap: The paper's core idea is to replace exhaustive path accounting with many random trials that imitate the way path evidence would accumulate. This is the Monte Carlo idea: when an exact count is too expensive, sample many small random cases and average them so the repeated pattern becomes visible. Here the random cases are walks on the graph. A walk starts at a node and follows links step by step according to chance. By observing many such walks, the algorithm estimates how much path-based centrality credit nodes should receive without enumerating every path directly. The paper proposes two algorithms. MC-Katz approximates truncated Katz centrality, where the path evidence is deliberately stopped after a bounded length. MC-KatzP approximates the original form. The important engineering move is that random walks can be run mostly independently, so many workers can generate samples at the same time and then combine their counts.
906.mech: The mechanism begins with a graph and a chosen Katz centrality target. The graph supplies the allowed moves: from a node, a random walk can follow one of the node's links to another node. For the truncated version, the method only needs to consider walks up to a limited length, because that version of the score intentionally ignores longer paths. For the original version, MC-KatzP must approximate the full Katz idea rather than only the bounded form, though the abstract does not describe the stopping rule or sampling details. The algorithm launches many random walks. Each walk is a small experiment: start somewhere, move along links, and record which nodes are reached or how much centrality credit is produced by the visited path. Because one walk does not need to know the choices made by another walk, the work can be split across processors. After enough walks have been simulated, the separate evidence is combined into estimated scores. Those scores are then used in two ways. First, they approximate the numeric Katz centrality values, measured in the abstract by low mean relative error. Second, they sort nodes so the most influential ones rise to the top. The output is therefore not only a table of approximate scores, but also a practical ranking of important nodes.
906.math: The first mathematical object is a graph: a set of nodes and links. Katz centrality is a path-counting score. It asks, in effect, how much evidence reaches a node through many possible walks, while not treating all walks as equally valuable. This is richer than degree, which only counts direct links, because it gives a node credit for being connected through chains of relationships. The second idea is approximation by sampling. Instead of counting every possible path, the algorithm samples random walks. A random walk is a chance process on the graph: at each step it chooses a link and moves. The law behind this is averaging repeated trials. One walk is noisy and may land in an unrepresentative place, but many independent walks reveal stable frequencies. The third idea is ranking. The exact score is useful partly because it orders nodes by importance, and the abstract emphasizes accuracy in ranking the most influential nodes. The fourth idea is parallel computation. The samples are independent enough that different workers can run them separately, then merge their partial counts. The main tradeoff is speed versus precision: fewer samples are cheaper but noisier; more samples are closer to the intended score but cost more.
906.dots: This paper sits at the intersection of network reasoning, ranking, probability, and efficiency. It is a network paper because links are the evidence: a node matters because of how paths reach it through the graph. It is a ranking paper because the final practical act is to sort nodes so influential ones can be found before less important ones. It is a probability paper because the method trusts repeated random walks to stand in for an enormous exact count. It also belongs to the efficiency and scalability family because the original measurement is already well defined, but the direct route is too expensive. Nearby centrality work in the repo asks related questions from different angles: some papers predict centrality in temporal networks, others examine how centrality can be manipulated by fake identities, and others use central nodes as landmarks for graph learning. This paper focuses on making one established centrality score computable at large scale.
906.ww: The approach should work because Katz centrality and random walks speak about the same underlying object: paths through a graph. Katz centrality values a node according to the pattern of walks that can reach it or pass through the graph around it. Random walks generate examples of those paths instead of listing them all. If a node is genuinely central under Katz's path-based view, many sampled walks should repeatedly expose that fact. A single walk is unreliable, but many independent walks reduce accidental noise because odd choices in one sample are balanced by other samples. Parallelism strengthens the practical case. The algorithm does not have to wait for one giant exact calculation to finish; it can divide the sampling work into many independent pieces and combine the results. That matches modern hardware better than approximation methods with shared bottlenecks. The method improves over the naive exact approach by avoiding exhaustive path computation, and it improves over weak approximations when it preserves the top-node ordering that users often care about most.
906.po: The payoff is a faster way to use Katz centrality on large graphs where exact computation is too costly. The abstract reports experiments on nine real-world datasets, with low mean relative error and high accuracy in ranking the most influential nodes. It also reports two to three orders of magnitude speedups over baselines, meaning roughly 100 to 1000 times faster. The practical capability is not a new definition of importance, but a more usable route to an existing one. Analysts can keep a path-sensitive centrality measure while paying a much lower computational price.
906.limits: The method depends on the graph's links being meaningful evidence about importance. If links are missing, fake, stale, or represent very different relationship types, a good Katz approximation can still rank the wrong nodes because the underlying graph is misleading. It also depends on enough random walks being sampled; too few samples can create noisy scores, especially for nodes whose importance is rare or path-dependent. The abstract reports low error and strong ranking accuracy on nine real-world datasets, but it does not prove the same behavior for every graph shape, every hardware setting, or every choice of Katz parameters. It also does not specify from the abstract alone how MC-KatzP controls the infinite-path nature of original Katz centrality.

907.bp: An e-commerce search page is no longer just a ranked stack of products. A shopper may see product tiles, brand blocks, images, modules, and visually different regions arranged across a two-dimensional page. The business question is therefore not only, "which product should be first?" It is, "what whole page should this shopper see so the page feels useful now and still leads to satisfaction later?" The paper serves the people who design search result pages where attention is split across rows, columns, and visual elements. A product can be relevant in isolation but less useful if its placement makes the page repetitive, confusing, or too focused on a short-term sale. The abstract says the authors build a whole-page experience optimization approach for e-commerce search, explicitly tying item relevance, page layout, and visual presentation to long-term customer satisfaction rather than only clicks or same-day revenue.
907.wh: The hard part is that the page creates effects that a simple list model cannot see. Traditional rankers often assume users scan results in a mostly linear order, so they correct for position bias: the top item gets more attention partly because it is high, not necessarily because it is better. But a modern search results page is non-linear. Items sit in a two-dimensional layout, visual blocks pull the eye differently, and one item can change how a nearby item is perceived. The second difficulty is time. Clicks and same-day revenue arrive quickly, so they are tempting targets. Expected two-week revenue and longer satisfaction arrive late, after many other events may have happened. That creates a credit problem: when satisfaction appears later, the system must decide which earlier page decision deserves credit. The paper is hard because it tries to optimize a spatial experience using delayed evidence.
907.naive: A smart beginner would take the existing product ranker, sort items by predicted relevance or immediate revenue, and then fill the page from top left to bottom right. They might add a simple correction for top positions, because higher slots naturally get more attention. This fails in two ways described by the abstract. First, a two-dimensional page is not a straight list, so the model misses how layout and visual elements shape attention. Second, short-term signals such as clicks and same-day sales may reward pages that look successful today while weakening longer satisfaction, brand relevance, or two-week value. The beginner method measures what is easy to see soon, not what the whole page caused over time.
907.ap: The core move is to treat the search results page as one designed experience rather than as a container that passively receives a ranked list. The approach does not ask only whether item A should appear above item B. It asks how item relevance, two-dimensional placement, and visual elements work together. That means the controllable object is the whole page: which products are shown, where they sit, and how their visual presentation affects the user's experience. The second move is measurement. Because long-term satisfaction cannot be read from an immediate click, the paper uses causal reasoning with quasi-experimental data to build metrics that stand in for long-term satisfaction, including expected two-week revenue. The system then optimizes against these broader signals and validates the result in a live industry-scale A/B test, where the abstract reports gains in brand relevance and revenue.
907.mech: The mechanism starts with a search request and a set of candidate items that could appear on the results page. For each candidate, the system needs evidence about relevance: how well the item fits the shopper's search intent. But the paper says relevance alone is not enough, so the system also represents the page as a two-dimensional layout with positions and visual elements. Instead of scoring every item as if it lived alone in a vertical list, the whole-page approach scores configurations of items and presentation choices together. A page choice is good only if the selected items, their locations, and their visual treatment jointly improve the experience. The delayed-outcome part then adds another layer. The system cannot simply wait two weeks for every decision before learning, so the authors use quasi-experimental data: naturally occurring or designed comparisons that make some page differences more fairly comparable than raw logs. From these comparisons, a causal measurement step estimates long-term satisfaction metrics, such as expected two-week revenue, by asking what later outcome is attributable to the earlier page experience rather than to unrelated shopper or market differences. The optimization step uses those metrics to prefer whole-page layouts that balance relevance, visual experience, and long-term value. The output is not merely a sorted list; it is a search results page arrangement intended to perform better as a full page.
907.math: The main mathematical ideas are ranking, page-level optimization, delayed credit assignment, and causal comparison. Ranking turns many candidate products into an order or selection under limited attention, but here the paper stretches ranking beyond a one-dimensional list. The page is a structured object: items occupy spatial slots, and visual elements change how attention moves. Optimization means defining what counts as a better page and searching among possible page arrangements for choices that raise that score. The danger is that the easiest score, such as immediate clicks or same-day revenue, may not be the true target. Delayed credit assignment is the problem of connecting an outcome that appears later to the earlier decision that may have caused it. Causal comparison addresses that by asking a stricter question than correlation: among comparable cases, what changed when the page experience changed? Quasi-experimental data is useful because it gives partial substitutes for a perfectly randomized experiment, creating more credible comparisons than ordinary behavior logs. The tradeoff is measurement trust versus deployment practicality. Waiting for clean long-term randomized evidence everywhere would be slow, but optimizing only quick signals would steer the system toward shallow wins.
907.dots: This paper sits in the repo's advertising and e-commerce family because it is about making a marketplace decision more faithful before acting on it: what should be shown, where, and according to which customer goal. It is also part of the search and ranking thread, since the system must choose a small visible page from a much larger product pool. What makes it different from ordinary retrieval is that the chosen objects interact on the page; visibility is spatial and visual, not just ordinal. It connects to the causal-inference family because the paper does not trust raw clicks or revenue as direct proof. It asks what the page experience caused, using quasi-experimental evidence to estimate longer satisfaction. It also neighbors conversion and recommendation work in the repo, where delayed feedback, price variants, suppression decisions, and query expansion all show the same pressure: a commercial system must optimize user value without mistaking easy short-term behavior for the real outcome.
907.ww: The approach should work better than the naive rank-and-fill strategy because it matches the object being controlled. If the real product is a whole search results page, then optimizing isolated item scores throws away information about layout and visual context. A page can fail even when many individual items are relevant, for example if the visual arrangement makes the experience cluttered or if valuable brand-relevant content is placed where users do not meaningfully attend to it. Modeling the interplay among relevance, position, and visuals gives the system a way to avoid those page-level mistakes. The causal measurement also improves the learning target. Raw clicks and same-day revenue are fast but biased toward immediate reactions. By estimating longer satisfaction from quasi-experimental comparisons, the system can reward page choices that continue to matter after the session. The A/B test evidence in the abstract supports this intuition: the optimized pages increased the primary customer experience metric, brand relevance, while also producing a statistically significant revenue lift.
907.po: The payoff is a search optimization system that treats the search results page as a designed surface, not a one-column ranking problem. According to the abstract, the industry-scale A/B test showed a 1.86% improvement in brand relevance, which the authors identify as their primary customer experience metric, and a statistically significant revenue uplift of 0.05%. The practical capability is important because it suggests a commerce platform can improve longer customer experience without giving up revenue. It also gives the platform a way to reason about visual page layout and delayed satisfaction inside the same optimization loop.
907.limits: The abstract does not reveal the exact model form, feature set, quasi-experimental design, or how expected two-week revenue is estimated, so the strength of the causal claim depends on details not shown here. The approach assumes the quasi-experimental comparisons are fair enough that hidden differences between users, queries, products, or time periods do not explain the measured gains. It also assumes brand relevance is a trustworthy customer experience metric and that the A/B test setting represents future traffic. The reported 0.05% revenue lift is statistically significant, but the abstract alone does not show its business variability, segment effects, or whether some query types or sellers lose while the average improves.

908.bp: A large recommender is trying to answer a simple question under severe time pressure: after seeing what a person has done before, what should it show next? For videos, products, or news, a long history is valuable because old actions can reveal durable interests that a short recent window misses. A person who buys camping gear every spring or repeatedly watches cooking clips may carry that preference across many sessions. The paper starts from the tension that generative recommenders, which produce or score next-item choices from a user's ordered past, tend to get better when they can read longer histories, but reading more history costs more computation at serving time. Real deployment cannot spend unlimited time on each recommendation moment. This work serves the practical need to keep the long-term preference signal while shortening what the model must process, using item categories as a compact substitute for many repeated item-level events.
908.wh: The hard part is that a user history is both useful and bulky.
