If the system keeps every past item, it preserves detail: exact products, exact videos, and the order in which interests appeared. But every extra event gives the recommender more material to process before it can answer, which is exactly what hurts real-time use. If the system simply cuts the history down to a short recent tail, it becomes cheaper but may forget stable preferences that live farther back. If it randomly samples old actions, it may keep many near-duplicates while dropping the one event that signals a rare but important taste. The abstract points to item categorical features as the available structure. Categories create a middle path, but they are also risky because many different items can share one category. The challenge is compressing repeated categorical evidence without flattening the user's interests into a vague popularity profile.
908.naive: A smart beginner would set a fixed maximum history length and keep only the most recent interactions. That is easy to deploy because the model sees fewer events, and recent behavior often matters. It fails when long-term interest is not the same as immediate activity. A user may browse gifts today but still prefer sports equipment, mystery novels, or budget hotels over months. Another beginner move would be to merge everything in the same category into one crude count. That saves even more work, but it can erase order and item differences. The paper's abstract suggests why both simple moves are incomplete: longer sequences improve generative recommendation, so the useful signal is in the long record, yet that record must be shortened before real-time serving becomes practical.
908.ap: The core idea is to compress the user's long sequence by using a piece of structure that items already carry: their categories. Instead of treating the history as a long chain of unrelated item identifiers, the method groups or summarizes parts of the history through categorical features so repeated evidence about the same kind of interest does not have to be represented by many separate events. The aim is not to invent a new source of preference information; it is to preserve the preference information already present in the history while removing avoidable processing cost. In concrete terms, if many past actions point to the same broad interest, the compressed sequence can carry that interest with fewer units. The generative recommender then receives a shorter user record that still says what kinds of things the person has cared about, allowing it to recommend under a tighter serving budget.
908.mech: The input is a long-term user history: an ordered list of items the person interacted with, plus categorical features attached to those items. The paper title and abstract do not specify the exact compression rule, so the safe description is at the level the evidence supports. First, the system reads the long sequence and looks at the categories associated with the items. Second, it uses those categories to identify parts of the history that carry overlapping preference evidence. Several item events can then be represented more compactly because their shared category says they point to a similar kind of user interest. Third, the method builds a shorter sequence that is meant to retain the interests expressed by the original long record while dropping redundant detail. Fourth, this compressed sequence is fed to a generative recommender, the kind of model that uses the user's past sequence to produce or score likely next items. Fifth, the recommender works over fewer sequence elements, so each user request requires less computation. The output is still a recommendation decision, but the serving path has changed: rather than asking the model to read the whole long history item by item, the system gives it a category-informed shorter memory. The experiments compare this compressed-history approach with the influential HSTU model on two large-scale datasets, reporting lower cost and higher accuracy at comparable sequence length.
908.math: The main mathematical idea is compression, meaning the act of keeping the information that matters for a task while using a smaller description. Here the scarce resource is computation during real-time recommendation, and the thing being compressed is an ordered user history. The compression is guided by categories, which act as shared labels over items. A category is a coarse partition: it says several items belong to the same kind of object, so some differences between them may be ignored when the goal is to remember broad interest. That creates a tradeoff between detail and cost. Keeping every item preserves fine distinctions but makes the model slow. Keeping only categories is cheaper but may blur items that differ inside the same category. The paper's move lives between those extremes by using categorical features to shorten the sequence while preserving user interests. Sequence modeling is the second idea: the order of past actions matters because the next recommendation depends on the path that led to the present. Ranking is the final idea: after the compressed history is read, candidate items must still be placed in an order. The reported accuracy gains mean the shortened record helped put better candidates higher, at least in the tested datasets and cost comparisons.
908.dots: Inside the repo's recommender-systems family, this paper sits in the branch concerned with making selection affordable without losing the candidates that matter. It is close to long-behavior and pre-ranking work because all of them face the same operational pressure: a recommender must choose from a huge item pile while spending only a small amount of time per request. It is also directly tied to the sequence concept. A user's history is not a flat pile of clicks; the order and recurrence of actions reveal both stable interests and recent direction. The information concept is another neighbor because the method asks which parts of a long record change the recommendation enough to deserve storage and which parts are redundant. Compared with cold-start recommendation in the same batch, this paper handles the opposite case: not too little history, but too much history to process cheaply. Compared with e-commerce search ranking, it shares the same final act of ordering candidates under limited user attention.
908.ww: The reason this can work is that user histories contain repeated structure. People often interact with many items that differ in identity but point to the same broader interest. If the recommender has to process every one of those events separately, it pays for repeated evidence again and again. Categories provide a cheap clue about redundancy: when many items belong to the same category, the system can often keep the signal that the user cares about that kind of thing without preserving every item-level occurrence. This should improve over a short-tail cutoff because older categorical evidence can survive compression instead of being discarded wholesale. It should improve over uncompressed long histories in deployment because the model receives fewer elements and therefore spends less computation before producing recommendations. The approach depends on categories carrying real preference meaning. When they do, compression removes mostly repeated detail while leaving the structure that helps the generative recommender infer what the user is likely to want next.
908.po: The payoff is a cheaper path to long-history recommendation. The abstract reports that, on two large-scale datasets, the approach achieves up to a sixfold reduction in computational cost compared with HSTU. It also reports up to 39 percent higher accuracy at comparable cost, described as similar sequence length. Those claims mean the method is not only making the model faster by throwing information away; in the reported setting, the category-guided shortened history can be a better input than an equally short ordinary sequence. The practical capability is real-time serving with more of the user's long-term interest preserved than a simple short-window design would keep.
908.limits: The abstract does not prove that category-based compression will work for every catalog or every user. It assumes item categorical features are available and meaningful, and that users' important interests can often be preserved at the category level. That can fail when categories are too broad, noisy, missing, or misaligned with why people choose items. Two products in the same category may serve different budgets, styles, brands, or occasions. The abstract reports experiments on two large-scale datasets, but it does not specify long-term user satisfaction, fairness effects, cold-start behavior, or cases where rare item-level details matter. The source code availability helps reproducibility, but the abstract alone does not establish behavior across all real-time systems.

909.bp: The ordinary problem is deciding what would happen to one person, account, patient, student, or user if they received a treatment, message, product, or policy, when the evidence comes from a connected social or interaction network rather than from a clean experiment. The goal is an individual treatment effect: for each unit, estimate the difference between the outcome under treatment and the outcome without it. In a network, that question is not local. A person's treatment choice may depend on their own traits, on hidden traits, and on neighbors; their outcome may also be changed by what happens to neighbors. The paper serves settings where platforms or scientists observe past behavior but did not randomly assign treatment. It asks how to recover the hidden sources of bias well enough to compare like with like, while also respecting that connected units can spill influence onto one another.
909.wh: The hard part is that network data mixes several reasons into the same observed record. Some hidden reason may affect whether a unit receives treatment and also affect the outcome; that is confounding, because it makes treatment look helpful or harmful even when the hidden reason did the work. A second hidden reason may affect treatment assignment but not the outcome directly; that behaves like an instrument. A third may help adjust the outcome comparison without being the same as the treatment driver. Network links add another layer: neighbors can share hidden traits, and a neighbor's treatment or features can create spillover effects. If all observed variables are poured into one learned hidden description, the model may blur these roles together. Then the correction step can remove the wrong bias, leave the true bias in place, or mistake neighbor influence for an individual's own treatment response.
909.naive: A smart beginner would gather every observed variable for each unit, add some neighborhood summaries, train a predictor for treated and untreated outcomes, and read the difference as the individual effect. That sounds sensible because more variables should explain more of the outcome. It fails because prediction is not the same as a fair comparison. Variables that help predict treatment are not always the variables that bias the outcome comparison. Variables that predict outcomes may have nothing to do with why treatment was assigned. In a network, a neighbor's signal may be a real spillover path or just shared background. Treating all of these signals as one mixed description can hide the exact factor that must be balanced.
909.ap: The core idea is to split the hidden description of each unit into three compartments with different causal jobs. NDiVAE learns an instrumental factor, a confounding factor, and an adjustment factor instead of asking one hidden vector to explain everything. In plain terms, it tries to separate what mainly explains treatment assignment, what explains both treatment and outcome, and what helps adjust outcome prediction. It then lets network information enter through aggregated factor representations, so the model can use neighbors without pretending every neighbor signal has the same role. Sample reweighting is used to make treated and untreated cases more comparable under the learned confounding signal. Causal regularization, meaning extra training penalties that reward the intended separation, pushes the three compartments not to collapse back into one mixed bucket.
909.mech: The input is networked observational data: units, their observed variables, their links to other units, treatment assignments, and outcomes. The method first uses a variational autoencoder, which is a learn-and-reconstruct machine: it compresses the observed record into hidden factors and checks whether those factors still explain the data well enough. Unlike a generic compression, this one is structured. For each unit, it produces three hidden factors with assigned roles: one for treatment-related instrumental signal, one for confounding signal shared by treatment and outcome, and one for adjustment signal useful for outcome estimation. The graph part then gathers information from linked neighbors to form neighborhood-level versions of those factors. This matters because a unit's observed treatment and outcome can be shaped by connected units, not only by its own variables. Next, the outcome and treatment parts of the model are trained so the right factor influences the right prediction task. Sample reweighting changes how much each observed case counts, giving more weight to cases that help treated and untreated groups become comparable after accounting for learned confounding. Causal regularization adds explicit pressure for separation among the factors. The output is an estimated individual treatment effect for each unit, plus theoretical claims that the separated factors can be identified under stated conditions and that estimation error can be bounded.
909.math: The main mathematics is controlled comparison under hidden causes. For one unit, the desired quantity is the difference between two outcomes, but only one was observed. Causal inference builds the missing comparison by trying to hold background reasons steady while treatment changes. Confounding is the dangerous background reason: it affects both treatment assignment and outcome, so it can make an unfair comparison look meaningful. The paper's representation learning means learning compact hidden descriptions from many observed variables; the word hidden matters because the important factors are not directly recorded. A variational autoencoder uses probability to express this uncertainty: instead of claiming one exact hidden state, it learns plausible hidden factors that can generate the observed data. Disentanglement means assigning different hidden factors different jobs, so treatment-only information, shared treatment-outcome information, and adjustment information do not all occupy the same slot. Graph aggregation is network math: each unit's factors are revised using linked neighbors because links may carry spillover or shared background evidence. Reweighting is balancing: treated and untreated cases that were not naturally comparable are given weights so the comparison better resembles a fair one. The tradeoff is separation versus assumption. The factor split is useful only if the data and model constraints really make those roles distinguishable.
909.dots: In the repo's conference map, this paper sits at the intersection of causal inference and graph learning. The causal-inference family is about repairing broken comparisons before taking action; this paper repairs the comparison by learning which hidden factor must be balanced for individual treatment effects. The graph-learning family is about controlled evidence movement through links; here the links are not merely helpful context, because they can also create interference, where one unit's treatment affects another unit's outcome. It also connects to the network concept, which treats neighbors as evidence carriers whose messages must be limited and interpreted, and to the cause concept, which asks what would change if treatment changed while look-alike explanations were held apart. Compared with graph explanation papers that look for causal subgraphs, this paper uses graph structure to estimate treatment effects. Compared with recommender or fairness work that separates popularity or demographic shortcuts from preference, it separates hidden causal roles inside networked observational data.
909.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive approach because it matches the different jobs that signals perform in a causal question. If one mixed representation is asked to explain treatment, outcome, and neighborhood influence at once, the model has no strong reason to keep the bias-correction signal separate from harmless prediction signal. By learning a confounding factor directly, NDiVAE gives the reweighting step something more targeted to balance. By learning instrumental and adjustment factors separately, it reduces the chance that treatment-only information or outcome-helpful information is mistaken for the confounder. Neighborhood aggregation helps because network interference means a unit's outcome can depend on more than its own record; some neighbor evidence belongs in the estimate. Causal regularization helps by turning the intended causal roles into training pressure rather than a verbal hope. The theoretical identifiability claim is important for the same reason: it argues that, under conditions not fully shown in the abstract, the learned hidden compartments correspond to recoverable causal factors rather than arbitrary convenient summaries.
909.po: The payoff is a more careful way to estimate individual treatment effects from connected observational data. According to the abstract, NDiVAE addresses both confounding bias and spillover effects by learning three distinct hidden factors per unit, adding graph-based neighborhood information, reweighting samples, and enforcing causal separation. The claimed result is not just higher prediction accuracy; it is better identification of the factors needed for bias correction. The paper also reports theoretical guarantees through identifiability and a generalization error bound, and experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets demonstrating the method. That combination matters because treatment-effect estimates are only useful when a later decision can trust the comparison.
909.limits: The claims depend on the assumed factor structure being true enough: instrumental, confounding, and adjustment factors must be separable from the observed networked data. The graph links must carry relevant neighbor information rather than merely encode noise, selection bias, or unrelated contact. Reweighting helps only if the learned confounding factor captures the main unfair differences between treated and untreated units. The abstract is truncated after saying experiments demonstrate NDiVAE, so it does not show the complete empirical results here. It also does not prove from the abstract alone that the method transfers beyond synthetic and semi-synthetic settings, where the hidden causal structure may be cleaner than in real deployments.

910.bp: Imagine an industrial plant where many sensor readings arrive every second: pressure, flow, temperature, vibration, valve position, and other measurements. The practical question is not just whether the whole plant looks strange, but whether one particular measurement is drifting away from what its own history and related measurements make reasonable. N41 serves that warning problem for multivariate time-series data, where many ordered measurement streams move together over time. The paper's central concern is that a detector asked to reconstruct or predict many features at once may become too broad. It can look acceptable on average while doing a poor job on the one feature whose mistake matters for a warning. N41 reframes anomaly detection around one target feature at a time, while still letting similar neighboring features provide context. The goal is a more focused detector: one that knows which signal it is trying to explain and uses nearby signals only when they help explain that target.
910.wh: The hard part is that multivariate sensor data contains both dependence and distraction. A target feature usually does not move alone; a temperature reading may rise after a pressure change, and two related flows may share a daily rhythm. Ignoring other features throws away useful context. But using every feature as an output creates another problem: the model is trained to reduce an overall training error, so its effort is spread across many streams. A small feature-specific failure can be hidden inside a larger average. If one sensor is easy to predict and another is hard, the shared objective can spend too much attention on reducing the easy or dominant errors and not enough on the subtle target that would reveal an anomaly. The paper's tension is therefore focus versus context. A good detector needs related measurements, but it should not let unrelated outputs compete with the target for the model's limited error-reducing effort.
910.naive: A smart beginner would train one detector on the full multivariate series: feed in all sensor features and ask the model to output all of them. During normal periods, it learns the usual patterns; at test time, large prediction or reconstruction errors mark anomalies. This sounds natural because the plant is a connected system. The failure is that the training error is pooled across many outputs. The model is rewarded for doing well overall, not for doing especially well on each chosen feature. Some features may receive weak correction because their errors are diluted among many others. The beginner might then add even more features for context, but that can add noise and widen the same dilution problem.
910.ap: N41's core move is to split the broad detection task into focused target-centered tasks. For a chosen target feature, the model's output is only that single feature. Its input is not the entire multivariate record blindly, but the target's neighboring features, meaning features whose patterns are similar enough to be relevant. This changes what the model is being asked to care about. The training error no longer has to be shared across many output streams; every reduction in error is judged against the target. At the same time, the model is not forced to predict the target from the target alone. Neighboring features can carry evidence about normal movement, shared timing, and correlated changes. The paper presents this as a wrapper around any detection model: redefine the input and output around one target plus its neighbors, then let the underlying model learn that focused relationship.
910.mech: The mechanism begins with multivariate time-series data: many feature values observed in order. First, select one feature as the target, the reading whose normal behavior the detector should learn to explain. Second, identify neighboring features with patterns similar to that target. The abstract does not specify the exact similarity calculation, so the supported claim is the conceptual one: neighbors are chosen because their time patterns resemble the target and are therefore expected to contain relevant context. Third, build the model's input from those neighboring features rather than from an unconstrained pile of every feature. Fourth, set the model's output to the single target feature. During training, the detector adjusts its internal settings to make its target prediction or reconstruction error smaller. This is the error the abstract calls the loss function: a number saying how far the model's target output is from the target value it should have produced. Fifth, after training, the detector can score target behavior by how poorly normal target-centered expectations explain the observed target. Repeating this target-centered setup for different features gives each feature a detector whose learning pressure is concentrated on that feature rather than spread across many outputs.
910.math: Three mathematical ideas carry the paper. The first is error minimization: define a number that says how wrong the model is, then adjust the model to make that number smaller. In N41, the important change is what the error is about. If the output contains many features, the error is an aggregate across them. If the output is one target feature, the same learning process becomes a focused attempt to explain that target. The second idea is similarity. Neighboring features are useful only if their patterns are close to the target's pattern in the sense that their changes over time carry related evidence. Similarity is a compression: many detailed time movements are reduced to a judgment about which features are near enough to help, so the choice can miss unusual but useful relations. The third idea is relevance weighting by selection. Instead of giving every feature equal status, N41 lets only target-related neighbors enter the input. The tradeoff is accuracy versus distraction: enough context to explain the target, but not so many outputs or irrelevant inputs that the model's error-reducing effort is diluted.
910.dots: In the repo's current taxonomy, N41 belongs to the Time Series & Spatiotemporal family and overlaps with Fraud & Anomaly Detection. It shares the time-series concern that order matters: a sensor value is interpreted through how it changes over time, not as an isolated row in a table. It also shares the anomaly-detection concern of defining normal carefully enough that departures become visible. The local family notes place N41 near DESS, DynaME, ECLAD, and scalable stream anomaly detection, all of which deal with warning systems where normal behavior can be complex and moving. The mathematical tags in the repo connect it to following the slope downhill to improve, weighting the most relevant parts, and measuring similarity as nearness. Compared with forecasting papers that mainly preserve rhythms or fill missing values, N41 uses the same sequence evidence for a sharper purpose: make one target feature's normal behavior easier to learn, so abnormal behavior is less likely to be hidden by average multi-output success.
910.ww: The method should work when two conditions hold. First, a model trained on many outputs really does face competition among outputs: reducing one feature's error can matter less to the total training signal than reducing errors elsewhere. By making the target the only output, N41 changes the training pressure so every improvement is judged by the target alone. That gives subtle target-specific patterns a better chance to be learned. Second, neighboring features must carry useful shared structure. If a target normally rises after a related measurement rises, or if several sensors share a repeating operating pattern, those neighbors help the model tell expected movement from suspicious movement. The paper's design avoids two opposite mistakes: predicting the target in isolation, which lacks context, and predicting everything together, which spreads the error budget. Its reported F1 gains on the real-world HAI22.04 dataset support the idea that focused targets plus similar neighbors can reduce missed and false anomaly decisions compared with existing methods.
910.po: The payoff is a practical way to improve anomaly detection without requiring a completely new detector architecture. N41 redefines the problem around one target feature and its neighboring features, so the idea can be applied to any detection model according to the abstract. On the real-world HAI22.04 dataset, the paper reports F1 scores 1.7 to 7.5 times higher than existing methods. That matters because F1 combines two warning-system needs: finding real anomalies and avoiding too many false alarms. The capability gained is more target-sensitive monitoring in multivariate time-series data.
910.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. It does not state how neighboring features are selected, how many neighbors are used, or how stable those similarities are over time. The approach depends on the target having neighbors whose normal patterns are genuinely informative; if the useful cause is not similar in the chosen sense, selection may exclude it. It also assumes that single-target training improves detection more than it loses by not predicting multiple outputs jointly. The evidence named in the abstract is HAI22.04, so the reported gains do not by themselves prove the same size of benefit for every industrial system, sensor layout, or anomaly type.

911.bp: This paper serves systems that read text and turn it into structured records. In ordinary terms, the system must look at a sentence, find the words that name a person, organization, place, object, or event action, and then place those findings into boxes chosen by a human designer. Those boxes are called a schema: a rulebook saying which kinds of things count and what names should be used for them. The real problem is that different datasets and organizations use different rulebooks. A large language model can often understand the sentence itself, but it is asked to obey many competing local naming systems. The paper argues that information extraction needs two abilities that should not be tangled together: general reading ability, such as spotting the span of text that matters, and schema alignment, meaning the final mapping into one particular human-defined rulebook.
911.wh: The hard part is conflict between schemas, not merely lack of language understanding. If two datasets mark similar text with different category boundaries or names, joint training can teach the model contradictory habits. One schema may treat an event trigger as a narrow action word, while another may expect a broader phrase or a different event label. Adapting the model to one schema can then make it worse on another. The abstract calls this cost the schema alignment tax: the model pays for learning one local rulebook by losing accuracy under a different one. This is especially awkward for entity recognition and event detection because the same sentence contains both fairly universal clues and highly local labeling decisions. The universal part is finding the words that carry the event or entity. The local part is deciding which official category those words should occupy.
911.naive: A smart beginner would put many information extraction datasets together and train one large model to output every schema's labels directly. That sounds efficient because the model sees more examples and learns one unified task. It fails when the labels do not mean the same thing across datasets. The model is forced to memorize incompatible rulebooks inside one output behavior, so a choice that is correct for one schema may be wrong for another. Another beginner move is to tune the model separately for each schema. That avoids direct conflict, but it wastes the reusable reading ability and can hurt performance when the next dataset uses a new or slightly different schema.
911.ap: The core idea is to split extraction into three jobs: identify, conceptualize, and align. First, the large model focuses on finding spans, meaning the exact stretches of text that appear to name an entity or trigger an event. Second, it assigns each span a semantic concept, which is a meaning-level description before it is forced into one dataset's label vocabulary. Third, a smaller alignment model maps those concepts into the particular schema requested by a dataset or user. This changes the burden on the large model. It no longer has to carry every local rulebook as one tangled behavior. It learns the reusable parts of extraction, while lightweight models handle the final schema-specific translation. The abstract's important claim is that the first two phases can be reused across tasks.
911.mech: The input is text from multiple information extraction datasets, each with its own human-defined schema. The first phase, identification, trains a large language model to mark candidate entity spans and trigger spans. A span is simply a continuous stretch of words, such as a name or an action phrase, and a trigger is the word or phrase that signals an event. The paper uses cross-dataset annotation in this phase, which means evidence from several datasets is used to improve recall, or the chance that the system finds the relevant spans rather than missing them. After spans are found, the conceptualization phase asks the large model to attach semantic concepts to each span. This is a middle layer: the span is no longer raw text, but it is not yet forced into one schema's label set. Finally, the alignment phase trains different lightweight models for different schemas. Each small model receives the concept-level output and translates it into the labels required by its target rulebook. The output is therefore not one universal label list. It is a reusable extraction core plus separate schema adapters, so adding or changing a schema mainly affects the final mapper rather than the whole language-reading model.
911.math: The mathematical shape is a decomposition of one difficult mapping into three simpler mappings. A direct system tries to learn a single route from sentence to schema label. ICA inserts a shared middle description: sentence to spans, spans to concepts, concepts to schema labels. This is a factorization idea, meaning the system separates a problem into parts that can be reused and parts that must remain local. Learning from examples is still central: the model adjusts its behavior so found spans and assigned concepts match annotated data. But the error being reduced is different in each phase. In identification, wrongness means missing or wrongly placing a span. In conceptualization, wrongness means attaching the wrong meaning-level concept. In alignment, wrongness means mapping a concept to the wrong schema label. There is also a similarity idea underneath the concept layer: different surface phrases and dataset labels can be treated as related when they point to the same underlying meaning. The main tradeoff is generality versus specificity. A very general extractor transfers well but may ignore local schema details. A schema-specific extractor follows local rules but can conflict with other schemas. ICA tries to put the stable meaning in the shared phases and the unstable rulebook choices in small adapters.
911.dots: In the repo's current JSON, this paper sits naturally with the text-mining and NLP family because it turns messy language into a usable decision rather than treating words as the final product. It also connects to the learning concept: the useful rule is too tangled to hand-code, so the system learns from annotated examples while trying not to learn accidental schema conflicts as permanent truth. The similarity concept appears in the conceptualization phase, where different spans or labels must be compared by meaning rather than by exact wording. The information concept appears in the separation between spans, concepts, and labels: each phase keeps the signal needed for the next phase while dropping detail that would create schema conflict. Nearby batch papers show related pressures. The NER self-training paper also worries about extracting named entities under limited trustworthy labels, while the structured RAG tutorial emphasizes that language systems must respect external structures such as schemas.
911.ww: The approach should work better than the naive direct model because it matches the source of the conflict. Finding the text span is often more stable than naming it under a particular schema. Many datasets may agree that some words refer to an organization or that a verb phrase triggers an event, even if they disagree about the final label or boundary convention. By training the large model on the reusable reading steps, ICA lets cross-dataset evidence improve span recall instead of turning every dataset difference into a fight inside one output space. The concept layer gives the system a buffer between text and schema. A concept can carry the ordinary meaning of a span before a small adapter decides how that meaning should be expressed in one local rulebook. Lightweight alignment models are easier to specialize because their job is narrower: translate concepts to labels, not relearn language understanding. This separation reduces the schema alignment tax by preventing schema-specific choices from corrupting the shared extraction ability.
911.po: The payoff is a more reusable information extraction system for settings where schemas change or conflict. Instead of retraining or retuning the whole language model whenever a new dataset rulebook appears, the first two phases can be reused and a lightweight alignment model can handle the new mapping. The paper targets unified entity recognition and event detection, so the practical benefit is broader than one label set. Grounded in the abstract, the claimed capability is better behavior under unseen schemas and less performance drop when multiple schemas are involved. That matters for organizations that need structured records from text but cannot force every dataset or department to share one labeling scheme.
911.limits: The abstract does not give the exact concept inventory, the alignment model design, or the evaluation numbers in the provided input, so those details cannot be inferred here. The method assumes that useful semantic concepts can sit between raw spans and schema labels. If a schema encodes very local policy choices that are not captured by the concept layer, the adapter may still struggle. It also assumes the identification phase finds enough true spans; missed spans cannot be repaired later by alignment. Cross-dataset annotation helps recall only if the datasets provide compatible evidence about what counts as a span. The approach reduces schema conflict, but it does not prove that every unseen schema can be handled with a small mapper.

912.bp: Named entity recognition is the job of reading text and marking spans such as people, organizations, places, products, diseases, or other named things, then assigning each marked span the right type. This matters because many downstream systems first need to know what concrete objects a document mentions before they can search, summarize, link records, check compliance, or build a knowledge base. The difficulty is that high-quality hand labels are scarce. A person has to decide exactly where an entity starts and ends and what type it has, and doing that across many domains is expensive. The paper studies self-training, where a model uses a small labeled set plus a large unlabeled set by creating temporary machine labels for the unlabeled text. Its central need is not simply more data. It is a way to decide which machine-made labels are clean enough to teach from, because bad temporary labels can turn unlabeled data from a resource into a source of repeated mistakes.
912.wh: The hard part is that self-training is a feedback loop. A model trained on few labeled examples marks entities in unlabeled text, then those predicted labels are treated as extra training material. If the predictions are right, the model gets more practice. If they are wrong, the model learns its own errors as if they were facts. The abstract names this as confirmation bias: incorrect pseudo-labels increase errors. Named entity recognition makes this especially delicate because a mistake can happen in several ways. The system can miss an entity, mark too many words, mark too few words, or choose the wrong type. A confidence score alone is not always enough, because models can be confidently wrong on unfamiliar names or sentence patterns. A large language model can bring outside language knowledge and few-shot judgment, but it can also hallucinate, meaning it may invent or overread labels not supported by the text. The paper is therefore trying to harvest unlabeled text without letting either the base model's confidence or the language model's fluent judgment dominate unchecked.
912.naive: A smart beginner would train a named entity recognizer on the small labeled set, run it over the unlabeled texts, keep predictions whose confidence is above a threshold, and retrain on those predictions. This is attractive because it is simple and cheap: the model supplies more labeled examples for itself. The failure is that confidence is not truth. A model can assign a high score to a wrong span because it has learned a shortcut from the small labeled set, such as treating a capitalized phrase as an organization in the wrong context. Once that wrong span is added to training data, later rounds can repeat and strengthen the shortcut. Another beginner move is to ask a large language model to judge all pseudo-labels. That also fails if its answer is accepted blindly, because the abstract worries about hallucinations.
912.ap: The paper's core idea is to make pseudo-label selection a judged and calibrated collaboration rather than a one-model vote. It introduces a large language model into self-training, but uses it specifically to select high-quality temporary labels for named entity recognition. The language model is prompted with a comprehensive instruction, and that instruction includes task rules mined by the language model itself from the limited labeled data. In plain terms, the system asks the language model to first help turn the few trusted examples into explicit rules about the task, then use those rules when judging proposed labels on unlabeled text. Because the language model can still hallucinate, the paper adds collaborative pseudo-label selection. It combines confidence from the recognizer with the language model's judgment, then uses calibration-guided probability smoothing to soften overconfident or poorly calibrated probabilities. The central move is to let outside language knowledge help, while requiring probability checks before machine-made labels become new training evidence.
912.mech: The input is a small set of labeled NER examples and a much larger set of unlabeled text. First, an initial NER model learns from the labeled examples. That model reads unlabeled sentences and proposes pseudo-labels: entity spans and their types that are not human-confirmed but may be useful. Second, the method prepares the large language model to judge those proposals. The prompt is not merely a generic question such as "is this label correct?" It is comprehensive and includes task rules mined by the language model from the labeled data, so the judgment is tied to the actual label definitions and examples available in this task. Third, for each proposed label, the language model supplies a quality judgment using its broad language knowledge and few-shot ability. Fourth, the system does not accept that judgment alone. It performs collaborative pseudo-label selection, combining the recognizer's confidence with the language model's judgment. Fifth, calibration-guided probability smoothing adjusts the probabilities. Calibration means asking whether a stated chance behaves like a trustworthy chance: predictions given high probability should be right more often than predictions given low probability. Smoothing means avoiding sharp, brittle probabilities when the evidence is uncertain. The output is a filtered set of higher-quality pseudo-labels. Those selected labels are then used in self-training so the NER model can learn from unlabeled text while reducing the chance that wrong machine labels dominate the next round.
912.math: The main mathematical ideas are learning from examples, probability as measured uncertainty, calibration, and weighted evidence combination. Learning from examples means the recognizer has adjustable rules for turning text into span-and-type decisions, and those rules are changed by comparing its output with labels. Self-training extends that idea by adding machine-made examples, but only if they are trustworthy enough. Probability appears because each pseudo-label is uncertain. A confidence score is a number saying how strongly the recognizer believes a span and type are correct, but the number is useful only if it matches reality often enough. Calibration is the check on that match: if many labels receive about 90 percent confidence, roughly that fraction should be correct in comparable cases. If the model is too sure, calibration-guided smoothing pulls the probability away from a brittle extreme. The large language model adds a second source of evidence. Its judgment is not a proof; it is another noisy signal built from language knowledge and the task rules placed in the prompt. Collaborative selection combines these signals so a pseudo-label is favored when the recognizer's score and the language model's rule-based judgment agree. The tradeoff is coverage versus cleanliness: accepting more pseudo-labels gives more training data, but accepting low-quality ones spreads errors.
912.dots: This paper belongs to the text-mining and language-model families in the repo because it tries to turn messy language into reliable structured decisions, not just produce fluent text. It is close to the broader learning-from-examples concept: the system has too few trusted labels, so it must reuse patterns from scarce examples without copying their accidents. It also sits near the probability concept, because the decisive question is not whether a label can be proposed, but how much uncertainty should remain before that label is trusted for training. The paper connects to other pseudo-labeling work in the current JSON data, including graph or multimodal entity alignment and fake-news adaptation papers that also worry about machine-made labels becoming harmful when coverage or confidence is poor. Its specific surface task is named entity recognition, but the deeper conference pattern is weak supervision under risk: use abundant unlabeled data, add a stronger judge or structural check, and prevent the loop from amplifying early mistakes.
912.ww: The method should improve over naive self-training because it attacks the exact place where self-training is fragile: the gate between a guessed label and a training label. The base recognizer supplies task-specific confidence because it has been trained on the labeled NER examples. The large language model supplies broader language knowledge, so it may notice that a phrase behaves like a person, organization, or location even when the small labeled set is thin. The mined task rules make that judgment less free-form by anchoring it to the labels and examples in this dataset. Collaborative selection then looks for agreement between different kinds of evidence instead of letting one source decide alone. Calibration-guided smoothing adds another safeguard: it treats probability as a claim that must be made less sharp when the model's confidence may not deserve full trust. This helps because confirmation bias grows from confident wrongness. By filtering pseudo-labels through both judgment and calibrated probability, the method tries to keep the useful extra examples while excluding the errors most likely to poison later training rounds.
912.po: The payoff is a self-training approach for named entity recognition that can make better use of limited labeled data and large unlabeled text collections. The practical capability is cleaner pseudo-label selection: the system can ask a large language model to judge candidate labels, guide that judgment with task rules mined from the few labeled examples, and reduce hallucination impact through collaborative confidence and probability smoothing. The abstract reports experiments on several NER datasets and says the method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. Grounded in the abstract, the main result is not a new entity type or a new dataset, but a safer way to decide which unlabeled examples should become training evidence.
912.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The limited labeled data must contain enough information for useful task rules to be mined; if the examples omit important entity types or boundary cases, the prompt can encode an incomplete view of the task. The large language model's judgments must contain real signal beyond fluent guessing, and its hallucinations must be frequent enough to need filtering but not so dominant that collaboration cannot rescue them. Confidence and calibration must track label quality in the tested settings. The abstract reports results on several NER datasets, but it does not prove behavior across every domain, language, entity schema, privacy setting, or adversarial text source. It also does not specify from the abstract alone how costly the language-model judging step is.

913.bp: Many knowledge-heavy applications now ask a language model to answer only after it has looked up outside material. That pattern, retrieval-augmented generation, is useful because the answer can be tied to documents, tables, graphs, or other records instead of coming only from the model's stored habits. This tutorial starts from a harder fact: real knowledge is rarely one flat pile of passages. A business database has tables and columns. A social system has people and links. A long report has sections inside sections. Each shape tells the system something about how evidence should be found and trusted. The practical need is therefore not just to fetch more context, but to build answer systems that understand the structure of the knowledge source and the risks that structure creates. The paper serves practitioners who need a map of this whole lifecycle, from structured evidence to final answers and safety defenses.
913.wh: The hard part is that structure is both helpful and dangerous. A table can answer precise questions, but only if the system respects rows, columns, and schema meanings. A social network can reveal nearby evidence, but links may spread misleading influence. A document tree can keep section context, but flattening it may separate a sentence from the heading that explains it. A plain retrieval system usually treats all stored material as comparable chunks, then ranks them by surface match to the question. That breaks when the useful clue is in a relation, a hierarchy, or a typed field rather than in matching words. Safety makes the problem sharper. In high-stakes settings, a bad retrieval path can support a plausible but wrong answer, and an attacker may exploit the structure itself by planting misleading records, links, or passages. The tutorial exists because these issues are scattered across different communities and designs.
913.naive: A smart beginner would build one general pipeline: cut every knowledge source into text snippets, search for snippets that resemble the user's question, paste the top ones into the model, and ask for an answer. This can work for simple factual lookup. It fails when the knowledge source carries meaning in its form. A database column name, a graph edge, or a document section boundary is not just extra decoration; it changes what a retrieved fact means. The same flat pipeline also misses structure-specific attacks. Poisoned table entries, misleading graph links, or malicious text hidden in a document branch can steer the answer while still looking relevant.
913.ap: The tutorial's central move is to treat retrieval-augmented generation as a structured knowledge problem rather than as text search followed by fluent writing. It surveys the full lifecycle of these systems and asks, at each stage, what kind of object the system is handling. If the outside knowledge is tabular, the design must preserve field meanings and schema relations. If it is a social network or knowledge graph, the design must reason over linked entities and decide which paths carry useful evidence. If it is a document tree, the design must keep parent-child context and section boundaries. The tutorial also puts safety into the same structural view. It does not treat attacks and defenses as an afterthought; it asks how the shape of the source changes what can go wrong and what protection should inspect.
913.mech: The mechanism described by the abstract is a teaching workflow, so the moving parts are design principles rather than one new algorithm. The input is a knowledge-intensive task plus an outside knowledge collection whose shape matters: tables with schemas, social networks with links, document trees with hierarchy, or other structured sources. First, the system must represent that source without erasing the signals carried by its form. A table needs names, fields, and relations between fields; a network needs nodes and links; a tree needs section order and nesting. Second, the retriever must choose evidence using the right unit. It may need a row, a linked neighborhood, a path, a subtree, or a passage with its heading, not just a loose text fragment. Third, the generator receives selected evidence and turns it into a downstream task solution, such as an answer or decision support. Fourth, safety checks ask whether the selected evidence can be trusted, whether the structure was manipulated, and whether the generated response is overconfident. The output of the tutorial is not a single prediction; it is a structured map of canonical designs, specialized designs for different knowledge forms, and attack and defense strategies.
913.math: The main mathematical idea is structured evidence selection under uncertainty. In plain terms, the system has many possible witnesses, and it must decide which witnesses deserve to shape an answer. With a table, the mathematical object is a set of records organized by fields; comparison means matching the question to the right fields and values while preserving how columns constrain one another. With a graph, the object is a set of nodes joined by links; the key question is how far evidence should travel along links before nearby help becomes distant noise. With a document tree, the object is a nested order; a child passage may depend on its parent heading, so removing hierarchy can change meaning. Ranking appears because only a small amount of evidence can be placed before the generator, so candidates must be ordered by usefulness and risk. Probability enters as disciplined uncertainty: the system should notice when evidence is incomplete, conflicting, or suspicious rather than treating a fluent answer as proof. Security adds an adversarial version of the same math: a record is not merely useful or useless, but may be crafted to redirect retrieval, pollute a path, or cause unsafe generation.
913.dots: This paper sits in the retrieval-augmented generation family, where many 2026 papers ask how an answer system should choose and govern outside evidence. Its distinctive role is broad and structural: instead of focusing only on conflict, confidence, document quality, graph search, or cost, it explains how those concerns change when the source is a table, network, or tree. It connects directly to information retrieval because the system must select a small useful set from a large store. It connects to graph reasoning because social networks and linked knowledge make evidence travel through relationships. It connects to ranking because retrieved candidates must be ordered before the generator can use them. It also connects to security and privacy-adjacent work because high-stakes use turns retrieval into an attack surface. The abstract frames the contribution as a tutorial that organizes fragmented work into a lifecycle view, not as a paper claiming one new experimental result.
913.ww: The approach works as a conceptual guide because it starts from what the evidence is made of. A flat text-only view forces every source through the same narrow doorway, so important constraints disappear before retrieval even begins. A structural view keeps those constraints available. In a table, field names prevent the system from confusing one kind of value with another. In a graph, links let the system look for supporting or neighboring facts when one isolated record is too thin. In a document tree, hierarchy keeps a paragraph tied to the section that gives it scope. These structures also tell defenders where to look. If an answer depends on a suspicious graph path, a strange table cell, or a document branch that carries hidden instructions, the safety problem has a concrete location. The gain is not magic accuracy; it is better bookkeeping over evidence, so retrieval, generation, and safety checks can use the same map of how knowledge is organized.
913.po: The payoff is a rigorous teaching map for people building retrieval-augmented systems on real structured knowledge. According to the abstract, the tutorial covers the full lifecycle, canonical designs, specialized principles for different knowledge structures, applications, and security attack and defense strategies. That buys a more disciplined way to decide how to model tables, networks, and document trees before using them to support generated answers. It also helps make safety specific: the system can ask what risks belong to this structure instead of applying one generic checklist to every knowledge source.
913.limits: The abstract describes a six-hour tutorial, so it does not prove a new method, report controlled results, or show that one design is best across all settings. Its claims depend on the surveyed work being representative and on practitioners being able to map their own data into the structural categories discussed. The structural view also assumes that schemas, links, and hierarchies are meaningful and available. If they are stale, incomplete, noisy, or deliberately manipulated, structure can mislead as much as it helps. The abstract mentions high-stakes safety, but it cannot by itself establish deployment readiness for medical, financial, legal, or security systems.

914.bp: The real object in this paper is a matrix: a rectangular grid of numbers that may stand for an image, a signal, or any record where rows and columns interact. Matrix deflation asks whether that grid can be peeled apart into simple layers. Each layer is rank-1, meaning it can be made by multiplying one column-shaped pattern by one row-shaped pattern, so every cell in the layer follows one shared row-column rule. Classical numerical methods can do this, but they usually need a stopping rule: after enough layers have been removed, the remaining grid is declared small enough or noisy enough to ignore. This paper asks whether a small team of AI agents can make that peeling decision more adaptively. A language model proposes the next simple layer, while a vision-language model judges whether the proposed layer and the remaining grid still look like meaningful structure rather than leftover noise.
914.wh: The hard part is not only finding one simple layer. It is knowing when the remaining grid still contains real structure. A fixed norm threshold measures the size of the leftover grid, but size and meaning are not the same thing. Random Gaussian noise can have measurable size without carrying a coherent pattern. A faint digit-like or image-like residue can be small but still meaningful. Different datasets also change the scale of the problem: an 8 by 8 digit, a 32 by 32 grayscale CIFAR-10 image, and a synthetic 16 by 16 matrix do not make the same visual or numerical demands. Noise makes the stopping problem sharper because every extra peel can start explaining noise as if it were signal. The abstract's central tension is therefore accuracy versus judgment: a purely formulaic rule is consistent, but it may stop too early, continue too long, or require a threshold tuned for one setting.
914.naive: A smart beginner would run ordinary singular value decomposition, remove the largest rank-1 slice, compute the size of what is left, and stop when that size falls below a fixed fraction of the original grid. That is close to the target used for Digits and CIFAR-10 in the abstract, where deflation stops when the Frobenius norm reaches 10 percent of the original. The failure is that the rule treats all leftovers with the same size as equally meaningful. It cannot tell a structured remnant from visually incoherent noise. It also requires choosing the threshold before seeing how noise, permutations, or dataset type change what the remainder means.
914.ap: The core idea is to replace one preset stopping number with a loop of proposal and judgment. The solver large language model, a text-based model used here as the proposing agent, generates a rank-1 singular value decomposition update. In plain terms, it suggests the next simple row-column layer to remove from the current grid. The vision-language model, a model that can judge visual structure as well as text instructions, accepts or rejects that update and decides when the process should stop. The paper also improves solver stability with in-context learning, meaning the solver is shown examples or instructions inside the prompt so it behaves more consistently during the current task. Row and column permutations are used to rearrange the grid so coherent visual structure is easier to see. The method is therefore agentic not because it is mysterious, but because separate agents take separate roles in an iterative numerical task.
914.mech: The mechanism starts with one matrix, such as an 8 by 8 Digits example, a 32 by 32 grayscale CIFAR-10 example, or a synthetic 16 by 16 matrix, sometimes with Gaussian noise added. The current matrix is shown or described to the solver model. Before solving, rows or columns may be permuted, which means their order is rearranged. This does not invent new numbers; it changes the display so repeated row-column structure can become visually coherent rather than scattered. The solver then proposes a rank-1 SVD update: one simple slice intended to capture a dominant pattern in the current grid. That slice is subtracted from the matrix, leaving a residual, the part not yet explained. The vision-language model then inspects the proposed update and the residual. It can accept the update if the slice appears to remove meaningful structure, reject it if the update is not useful, and decide whether the residual has become mostly noise. If accepted, the residual becomes the next input and the loop repeats. If the visual judge stops, the accepted slices form the decomposition and the final residual is what the method leaves unexplained. Evaluation compares this agentic result with numerical deflation targets: known construction rank in synthetic noisy cases, and a 10 percent Frobenius-norm target for Digits and CIFAR-10.
914.math: The central mathematical object is a matrix, a grid whose entries are not independent when there is structure. A rank-1 slice is the simplest structured grid: every row is a scaled version of the same row pattern, or equivalently every column follows one shared column pattern. Singular value decomposition is the classical way to express a matrix as a sum of such slices ordered by strength. Deflation means subtracting one slice at a time and asking what remains. The Frobenius norm is a single size measurement for a matrix: square every entry, add the squares, and take the square root. It is useful because it gives a common ruler for leftover error, but it collapses shape into one number. This paper's mathematical bet is that shape matters. A residual can be large because it contains meaningful row-column structure, or large because noise is spread everywhere. Permutations are also mathematical operations: reordering rows and columns preserves the values while changing which patterns are visually adjacent. The tradeoff is compression versus detail. Rank-1 slices compress a grid into a few simple patterns, but stopping too late compresses noise as if it were signal. The agentic judge is used as a learned, visual stopping rule over that tradeoff.
914.dots: In the repo's current map, gid 914 is tagged with keeping only the few dimensions that matter, learning a function from examples, and smart random sampling and averaging; its theme is matrix decomposition. It also connects to the LLMs and language-models theme because a language model is not being used to write an answer, but to participate in a numerical procedure. It connects to multimodal and vision-language work because the stopping decision depends on visual coherence in the matrix display. It connects to efficiency and compression papers because rank-1 peeling is a way to keep a small set of important components instead of the whole grid. The neighboring idea is not recommendation or retrieval on the surface, but the deeper pressure is shared: choose the useful small set from a larger noisy object. Here the candidates are matrix slices, and the score is whether the remaining grid still contains structure worth keeping.
914.ww: The method should improve over the naive threshold rule when the visual shape of the residual carries information that a single size number loses. A fixed Frobenius-norm cutoff answers only, 'How much leftover energy remains?' The agentic loop can also ask, 'Does the leftover look organized enough to be signal?' That distinction matters in noisy synthetic matrices, where the abstract says the true construction rank is known and numerical deflation provides a noise target. It also matters for image-like matrices, where digits and grayscale objects have spatially coherent patterns while Gaussian noise does not. Row and column permutations help because some structure is easier to judge when similar rows or columns are placed near one another. In-context learning helps the solver because repeated examples inside the prompt can stabilize the form of the proposed rank-1 updates. The division of labor also fits the task: the solver proposes a concrete numerical slice, while the visual judge controls acceptance and stopping. The reported competitive results suggest that this learned judgment can approximate classical targets without hard-coding the same threshold as the decision rule.
914.po: The payoff is a threshold-free way to perform matrix deflation with agents. The abstract reports evaluation on Digits, CIFAR-10 grayscale matrices, and synthetic matrices, both clean and with Gaussian noise. In the synthetic noisy case, where the true construction rank is known, the best agentic configuration differs from the numerical noise target by only 1.75 RMSE. For Digits and CIFAR-10, the comparison target is defined by deflating until the Frobenius norm reaches 10 percent of the original. The practical capability is not that classical SVD disappears; it is that proposal, acceptance, and stopping can be coordinated by agents instead of by a fixed norm threshold.
914.limits: The abstract frames the work as preliminary, so the evidence should be read as an early demonstration rather than a settled replacement for numerical algorithms. The method assumes that meaningful matrix structure can be recognized through the visual presentation given to the vision-language model, which may fail when useful structure is not visually coherent. It also depends on the solver producing valid rank-1 SVD updates consistently, even under noise and different permutations. The reported datasets are small grids or image-like matrices, so the abstract does not prove behavior on very large scientific, recommender, or graph matrices. It also does not specify runtime cost, failure cases for rejected updates, or how sensitive results are to prompts and permutation choices.
